kept.heading: THE OPEN INTERNET IS CLOSING THE GAP WITH WALLED GARDENS (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Two-thirds of consumer attention sits on the open internet while only one-fifth of ad spend follows it there, and advertisers often pay more for equivalent reach inside walled gardens. The gap was never a supply problem, since open publishers collectively reach massive audiences, but fragmented technology and limited outcome visibility made that inventory harder to value.
kept.article_text:
Title: The Open Internet Is Closing The Gap With Walled Gardens

URL Source: https://www.adexchanger.com/content-studio/the-open-internet-is-closing-the-gap-with-walled-gardens/

Published Time: 2026-07-27T12:00:22+00:00

Markdown Content:
Monday, July 27th, 2026 – 8:00 am

SHARE:

Two-thirds of consumer attention lives on the open internet, [but only one-fifth of ad spend follows it there](https://www.thetradedesk.com/assets/global/documents/TTD-Sellers-and-Publishers-Report-May-2024.pdf). That gap is no accident. Walled gardens spent the past decade creating it.

But now the gap is about to close. Better data, real investment in AI, credible measurement and market consolidation are giving the open internet the tools to finally prove that it can compete with walled gardens on outcomes, not just reach.

Open internet publishers collectively reach audiences at a scale that exceeds any closed platform. Fragmented technology stacks, point solutions and limited visibility into outcomes, however, have made it structurally difficult for open internet players to connect the right advertiser with the right audience. Inventory that is fragmented or cannot demonstrate its value attracts less demand, which results in lower CPMs.

This spend imbalance partly comes down to pricing. Published benchmarks show advertisers pay roughly double on average for equivalent reach inside walled gardens compared to the open internet. But the imbalance is also a result of walled gardens using their reach and data power to attract more budget. The challenge for open internet players has never been supply, but rather the infrastructure and data required to show what that supply is actually worth.

Those weaknesses are now being solved.

[![Image 1](https://www.adexchanger.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Verve_July2026_600x300.jpg)](https://verve.com/)

## Outcomes now matter more than media costs

For most of the history of programmatic advertising, the dominant advertiser question was about cost-efficiency: How cheaply can I buy media? This shaped the entire technology stack – from DSPs and SSPs to exchanges and data – around cost reduction and scale and made walled gardens attractive for the same reason. Owning substantial publishing assets gave walled gardens the ability to deliver on that demand.

However, the question that leading advertisers should ask is changing. It’s no longer “How cheaply can I buy media?” but “What business result did this investment actually create?” Whether the objective is customer acquisition, market share, brand perception or sales, the conversation has shifted from media cost to measurable impact and outcomes. When outcomes are the currency, the ability to demonstrate performance matters more than cheap inventory, and the open internet has a stronger performance case to make.

## Trust in walled gardens is eroding

For years, walled gardens were treated as the reliable part of the programmatic spectrum – think precise targeting, easier attribution and measurable reach – which made it easy for advertisers and their agencies to spend substantial media budgets without having to deal with multiple smaller-scale open internet point solutions. But as the open internet improves its weaknesses and increases transparency, such as through [recent upgrades to supply-chain visibility](https://iabtechlab.com/press-releases/iab-tech-lab-announces-supplychain-v1-1-transparency-upgrade-to-strengthen-trust-in-the-open-internet/), the relative advantage of closed environments continues to narrow.

Even the platforms themselves appear to recognize the problem.

Advertisers are becoming more critical of the context in which their ads appear within walled gardens. In June, AppsFlyer [announced](https://www.adexchanger.com/daily-news-roundup/tuesday-23062026/) it had secured more than $1 billion in investment from Google, Meta, Moloco and Unity at a $2.7 billion valuation to build independent, AI-powered ad measurement. AppsFlyer stated publicly that none of the investors receives preferential access to its APIs, measurement signals, attribution logic or commercial terms. In short, four major ad tech players just paid a premium for a minority stake in measurement infrastructure they explicitly do not control, a concrete signal that they know grading their own homework is no longer sufficient on its own. Independent, verifiable measurement is a critical piece of shared infrastructure.

## The data advantage is narrowing

Advances in AI, contextual intelligence, SDK-driven intent signals, privacy-first identity solutions and access to search intent signals and LLM conversational data are giving open internet platforms meaningfully better tools to predict audience behavior and likelihood to convert, and to connect ad exposure to outcomes. As these capabilities mature, the distinction between open and closed ecosystems becomes less about data availability and more about how effectively signals are activated.

As we argued in our recent AdExchanger piece on [why the future of bidding won’t be won by DSPs alone](https://www.adexchanger.com/content-studio/the-future-of-bidding-wont-be-won-by-dsps-alone/), the supply side is no longer just a pipe. SSPs with direct publisher relationships and access to SDK-level data sit on genuinely predictive signal sets. This advantage only compounds as AI gets better at activating them.

## Integration is becoming the edge

The open internet ecosystem was built around a deliberate separation between buy-side and sell-side technology. That separation no longer makes sense. Visibility across both demand and supply, combined with eliminating the cost of unnecessary intermediary platforms, creates advantages that point-solution providers cannot easily replicate.

Stronger demand attracts better supply. Richer supply generates better data. Better data improves advertiser performance. The flywheel increasingly favors platforms that have invested in closing the loop across demand, supply, data and performance.

## Consolidation is accelerating

The open internet remains fragmented, but consolidation is already underway. As AI capability, measurement infrastructure and data partnerships become table stakes, the market is separating platforms that can operate at scale from those that cannot.

The result will be a smaller number of larger and more capable companies, ones that can credibly compete with walled gardens on outcomes while preserving the diversity and publisher plurality that make the open internet worth competing for.

The path forward will be determined by who builds the strongest connection between advertisers, publishers, data and verifiable outcomes. The open internet has always had the raw material. In the new intelligence era, open internet players with scale, rich data and an AI-first approach are closing the outcomes gap with walled gardens fast enough to give advertisers a real alternative.

For more articles featuring Remco Westermann, [click here](https://www.adexchanger.com/tag/remco-westermann/).

kept.heading: RETURN OF THE HEARTTHROB: WHY THE MEN OF THE EARLY AUGHTS ARE BOOKED AND BUSY IN ADVERTISING (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Brands are reviving early 2000s heartthrobs to tap into millennial nostalgia and drive engagement, especially with audiences like millennial moms who now have strong purchasing power. By recreating teenage fantasies and cultural moments, these campaigns trigger emotional memories that feel joyful and simple compared to today's complexity. This “nostalgia talent” strategy also resonates with Gen Z's interest in 2000s culture.
kept.article_text:
Title: Why early-aughts heartthrobs are booked and busy in advertising

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/heartthrob-marketing-chad-michael-murray-devon-sawa-nostalgia

Published Time: 2026-07-27T10:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
If a brand offered to make one of your teenage daydreams into reality, would you do it?

That’s a question that Erin Miller recently got to ponder. Miller, a millennial content creator who posts throwback skits under the handle @overthemoonfaraway on TikTok (where she has 3.1 million followers) and Instagram (where she has 1.5 million), was recently offered the chance to collaborate with PepsiCo’s Bubly and star in an ad opposite actor Chad Michael Murray, who won the hearts of thousands of teenage girls for his roles in shows like _One Tree Hill_ and _Dawson’s Creek_.

She took it.

In the resulting 85-second spot, which was released in late June, Miller, in character as a dorky teen, sips a Bubly and is transported from her bedroom, where she’s got a poster of the early-aughts heartthrob, to her daydream fantasy where Murray showers her with attention. Playing the stand-in for millennial women who once swooned over Murray was “very surreal” for Miller, who told us she was “barely acting” in the ad.

“Millennials immediately recognized the fantasy of it,” Miller told us. “It was about remembering what it was like to be 13. We all had celebrity crushes. We were all writing in our diaries and covering our bedroom walls with magazine pages and posters, and we would imagine what it was like if our teen crush magically appeared. That emotional memory is what people [connect] to.”

Bubly isn’t alone in tapping into that emotional memory, and is the latest brand to revisit teen heartthrobs of the ’90s and early 2000s. Nor is the brand alone in landing Murray; snack-food brand Snackish also got Murray to riff off of his role in the 2004 teen rom-com _A Cinderella Story_ in some recent spots.

As for the other heartthrob ads: Last summer, handbag and accessory brand Vera Bradley [tapped](https://people.com/devon-sawa-channels-his-90s-teen-star-for-vera-bradley-ad-11793296) actor Devon Sawa to revisit his heartthrob status (and haircut) to make one woman’s fanfiction from 2002 into a five-minute spot. This past fall, Panera worked with Jared Padalecki and Matt Czuchry of _Gilmore Girls_ fame on an ad that not-so-subtly [references](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EP4cF5IBuFM) their respective characters, Dean and Logan. And this spring, actor Adrian Grenier may not have reprised his role as Nate in _The Devil Wears Prada_ sequel—but he did score two ads, one for Jarlsberg cheese and another for Starbucks, both of which [reference](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MEcjAtFJbgA) his character in the original film. (We’d rather Grenier go back to his character Chase Hammond in 1999’s _Drive Me Crazy_,but that’s beside the point.)

Audiences who once harbored these celebrity crushes may be thanking brand marketers, but it’s not pure altruism to bring back the heartthrobs of yesteryear to target core audiences. Instead, the feelings that ’90s and early 2000s heartthrobs once evoked can serve as a potential nostalgia cheat code to win the attention and affection of millennials today.

“Everything is so complicated and so scary to people right now,” Kelly Bayett, co-founder and managing partner of production shop Love Song, told us. “What it does is it brings you back to what you felt joy from, and what felt simple, and it didn’t have political undertones, and it wasn’t complicated.”

## **The ‘millennial mom’ audience**

Katelyn Meola, brand marketing director for PepsiCo’s flavored sparkling beverages portfolio, told us that Bubly’s target audience—as well as the brand’s Melted Ice Pop flavor promoted in the spot—were well served by a nostalgic approach.

##### Get marketing news you'll actually want to read

Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides.

“The millennial mom is really our target for Bubly,” Meola said. “As we all are marketing social-first, these are those collective memories that we can all bond over…Not only was [Chad Michael Murray] in all of these shows back then, but he was beyond being on TV. He was on your wall. He was the poster boy of the era. There’s so many little inside jokes that we even lean into within the piece.”

Those inside jokes and ample references to the time period—which include capri pants, journal doodles, a well-timed _All-American Rejects_ needle drop, and frizzy hair—are all crucial details for the social-first advertising to win over intended audiences, hopefully make the content go viral, and fill comment sections, per Meola.

Creating content that will appeal to an audience with attention to detail and accurate references is part of the “brand-ertainment” social-first approach that Snackish is also looking to produce, Tara Bosch, founder of Snackish, told us. But the key, Bosch said, is finding a way to make that content evoke a true feeling and connection.

“For us with the heartthrob, it’s really that nostalgia and that feeling of your inner teenage girl squealing that…evokes this joy and excitement,” Bosch said.

## **Nostalgia, all the rage**

Evoking those feelings of joy and excitement goes beyond heartthrobs, too. Millennial mainstays like Hilary Duff and Lindsay Lohan have also been booked for recent campaigns that similarly channel the past.

Over the last six months, there’s been a “big push” for “nostalgia millennial talent,” Garrett Smith, agent, endorsements at UTA, told Marketing Brew. That millennial talent appeals to a generation where “the purchasing power is pretty substantial” at the same time that Gen Z is “interested in millennial culture, 2000s culture,” a convergence that has increased the relevance of millennial talent for brands, Smith explained.

Ashley Strom, senior director at Platinum Rye Entertainment, noted that nostalgia continues to drive many campaigns. Working with millennial talent who hit those nostalgia points allows brands to create marketing that has a “transportative quality” and create an emotional connection that also allows them to be in cultural conversation and pitch media outlets to get their ads to go further, Strom said, which likely makes it even more appealing to do so.

Of course, there are some heartthrobs who aren’t yet booked and busy—and who some marketers would love to see more of.

“Where is JTT?” Strom asked, referring, of course, to the actor Jonathan Taylor Thomas, best known for starring in the sitcom _Home Improvement_ and who became a prominent feature of teen magazines of the ’90s and early aughts. “If a brand could book him to come out of hiding, that would be hilarious.”

kept.heading: USE THE STEEL MAN TECHNIQUE TO PERSUADE PEOPLE WHO DISAGREE WITH YOU (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Steel manning improves persuasion by presenting an opposing argument in its strongest form before responding. It emphasizes understanding, validating concerns, and then offering a deeper perspective. Techniques like feel-felt-found build empathy and trust. Research shows addressing objections directly increases persuasion and credibility. Limits matter - only raise objections that can be answered and already exist in the audience's mind. This approach leads people toward a conclusion without forcing them to reverse their stance.
kept.article_text:
Title: Use the steel man technique to persuade people who disagree with you

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/steel-manning/

Published Time: 2026-07-20

Markdown Content:
If your visitors have objections, you need to present counterobjections. However, it’s not enough to present the counterobjections straight.

![Image 1: A man in armor.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/Steel-man.jpg)

To _steel man_ is to create a version of your opponent’s argument that’s even stronger than their own.

The solution comes from two (similar) approaches:

## Approach 1: Steel manning

The philosopher Daniel Dennett outlines an effective process for arguing with someone who has opposing views:

1.   Attempt to re-express the other person’s position so clearly, vividly, and fairly that they say, “Thanks, I wish I’d thought of putting it that way.”
2.   List any points of agreement (especially if they are not matters of general or widespread agreement).
3.   Mention anything you have learned from your target.
4.   Only then are you permitted to say so much as a word of rebuttal or criticism.

The first step of Dennett’s approach has been called _steel manning_. It’s the opposite of _straw_ manning, in which you misrepresent the other person’s position or argument so you can easily defeat it. In contrast to a straw man, a steel man is an _improved_ form of the other person’s views—one that’s harder to defeat.

## Approach 2: Feel–felt–found

Dennett’s approach overlaps with **the “feel–felt–found” technique** that is taught in many customer-support call centers:

1.   Demonstrate that you understand how the other person _feels_.
2.   Then, describe how you (or someone else) once _felt_ the same as the other person does.
3.   Finally, describe how your mind (or someone else’s) was changed, and what you instead _found_ to be true.

## Why these approaches work

Steel manning isn’t just good manners. It’s the strongest form of something persuasion researchers have measured for decades—the _two-sided argument_.

When you think about it, there are three ways to deal with an objection:

*   Don’t mention it.
*   Mention it, but move on without addressing it.
*   Mention it and address it.

Separate studies by Mike Allen (1991) and Daniel J. O’Keefe (1999) both landed on the same finding. **If you raise your customer’s objection and then answer it, you persuade more people than if you had never raised it.**

The evidence was slightly murkier for advertisers. Raising objections in ads didn’t reliably increase conversion, but it did build credibility and trust.

In marketing, you don’t need to follow Dennett’s four steps literally. The goal is to show that you understand your prospect’s objection so well that **they feel properly understood _before_ you answer it**.

## Steel manning in action: Domino’s cardboard pizza

In 2010, Domino’s put its own customer research on television. Real customer posts, on camera, saying what they actually felt. Comments included:

> “Domino’s tastes like cardboard.”

> “Mass produced, boring, bland pizza.”

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AH5R56jILag)

As the video shows, Domino’s didn’t just acknowledge criticism; they presented it more candidly than anyone expected. By giving voice to the strongest version of their customers’ objections before answering them, they made their response far more credible and [gave customers a new reason to choose it](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/mac-vs-pc-copywriting-friday/).

Objection. Counter-objection.

US same-store sales rose 14.3% in the first quarter of 2010. At the time, that was the largest quarterly same-store gain in quick-service restaurant history.

## How to apply the above approaches to conversion

The approaches above may sound subtle, but they are powerful.

In both of them, you don’t just present your counterobjection straight. (You don’t just say, “You’re wrong. Here’s the right answer.”)

Instead, you first demonstrate that you _understand_ the other person’s objection, you demonstrate that it’s valid, and then you explain why your counterobjection is a level of thinking _deeper_, not _shallower_, than the other person’s. (You effectively say, “I understand what you think, and why, but if you think further…”) This approach allows the other person to save face and not have to backtrack their thinking (which no one likes to do). At no point are they proven wrong; they just arrive at your verdict through extended thinking.

(Note that you’d get nowhere trying to _straw_ man your visitors’ views. Your visitors would simply think, “You don’t understand me.” _Straw_ manning only works by misrepresenting a _third party’s_ position. You could, of course, do that with your competitor’s arguments. But that’s not defensible, and the best persuasion is defensible.)

So, if your visitors have objections, don’t just contradict them. And certainly don’t ignore them. Address the elephant in the room. Explain why their current thinking is valid. Empathize with why they were reasonable in arriving at those conclusions. And then show them the additional thinking that leads from their conclusions to yours.

## When steel manning backfires

If you have read this far and thought _this sounds risky_, you are asking the right question. **So let us put your objection _more_ strongly than you did.**

_Every argument above is an argument for handing your visitor a reason to leave. You are being asked to print your worst review in your own advertising. Domino’s only got away with it by changing the recipe first. Most companies can’t do that, and the ones that try will simply have reminded a wavering buyer exactly why they were wavering. **The safe play is to sell your strengths and stay quiet about the rest.**_

That is the strongest version of the objection, and two parts of it are right.

*   **If you can’t win the objection, don’t raise it.** If the strongest version of your visitor’s objection is one you can’t honestly beat, voicing it just hands them a reason to leave. Focus instead on fixing your product.
*   **Don’t plant an objection your visitor never had.** Steel manning works on the objection already in the reader’s head. Raise one that never occurred to them, and you’ve introduced doubt for free. This is why [customer research](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/questions/) comes first. You need to [know which objections are real and common](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/diagnose-problem-solution/), not which ones are theoretically available.

Notice what those two limits have in common. Neither is an argument against steel manning. **Both are arguments for knowing which objection you are facing before you open your mouth, which is the same discipline, done earlier.**

What about the idea that simply raising a common objection will entrench it in your prospect’s mind? If you’ve done your research, you’ll already know what’s there. **Your silence won’t remove an objection; it will just rob you of a chance to counter it.**

The challenge steel manning sets is whether our customer hears our answers to their fears, or write their own.

kept.heading: OPTIMIZING CRAWL BUDGETS: WHAT'S NEW (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google's updated crawl budget guidance explains how sites can help Googlebot access and index important pages more efficiently. New sites start with limited crawl capacity, which can expand as they grow and maintain regular updates. The guidance covers improving site performance and organization while reducing unnecessary crawling. It also introduces 304 status codes as a way to save server resources on unchanged pages.
kept.article_text:
Title: Optimizing Crawl Budgets: What’s New

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/optimizing-crawl-budgets-whats-new

Published Time: 2026-07-27T10:00:44+00:00

Markdown Content:
Google’s newly updated “Crawling infrastructure” documentation includes “[Optimize your crawl budget](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawl-budget),” a section with pointers on how websites can expose more pages to the search giant’s bots. The topic is important, as pages must be crawled to appear in Google’s index and search results.

The documentation addresses the need for a “budget” given the sheer number of global URLs. A poorly organized website will likely take longer to crawl and thus have fewer [indexed pages](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/googles-index-now-powers-chatgpt).

Here are takeaways from the new guidelines.

### Google Guidelines

**Every new site starts with a “conservative” crawl budget.**When launching a site, start with a modest number of pages to ensure that “Google can cover all the important content without overloading your servers.”

**Over time, the crawl budget increases based on the site’s size and updates.**Regular updates (especially if automatically included in its XML sitemaps) encourage the Googlebot to return and likely increase the crawl budget over time.

Update your product inventory and your blog regularly and gradually. For example, instead of launching 100 products in one day, consider three per day for a month, roughly.

**Improving your site’s load time may increase its crawl budget.**We’ve long known that faster websites are better crawled. Monitor your [site’s performance](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/3-excellent-performance-testing-tools-from-google), and strive to [improve its speed](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/quickly-drop-seconds-sites-load-time).

**Popular pages receive more frequent crawls.**Googlebot crawls pages with many inbound links ([external](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/15-tools-for-link-building) and [internal](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/seo-10-faqs-for-internal-links)) more frequently.

Other ways to improve crawl frequency and speed:

*   Use the _disallow_ command in [robots.txt](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/seo-manage-crawling-indexing-with-robots-exclusion-protocol) to block pages you don’t want indexed or in SERPs. Examples could be pages for private logins, shopping carts, and those dynamically generated.

*   Remove or consolidate [duplicate content](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/how-google-detects-duplicate-content).

*   Avoid soft 404 pages (deleted pages that return a 200 code) as Googlebot will continue to crawl them. Return 404 or 410 responses if the pages no longer exist.

*   Avoid redirect chains (multiple redirects for a single page)

*   Use Search Console’s [crawl stats report](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/9679690) (_Settings > Crawl stats_) to monitor the crawl rate and problems encountered by Googlebot.

[![Image 1: Screenshot of a Crawl stats report.](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Crawl-stats-report-570x552.jpg)](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Crawl-stats-report.jpg)

Search Console’s “Crawl stats” report reveals crawl frequency and problems, if any. _Click image to enlarge._

### Beware ‘URL Caching’

Google has added a new “URL caching” recommendation to the guidelines:

_Support 304 (Not Modified) HTTP status codes. If a page hasn’t changed since Google last crawled it, returning a 304 code tells Google to reuse the cached version, saving your server bandwidth and resources._

My experience is to follow this recommendation only for unimportant pages, such as expired products and policy pages. Telling Google via a 304 code that a page is stale could affect its visibility in SERPs or even its index status.

![Image 2: Ann Smarty](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/userphoto/2425.jpg)

What you'll learn

See real LinkedIn profiles optimized for inbound tech jobs

I'll break down hand-picked examples of profiles that consistently attract recruiter outreach and explain why they work.

Learn the principles that make those profiles work well

You'll understand why those profiles signal credibility to the right people, so you can replicate it in your profile.

Get live feedback on your profile during the call

Share your profile and watch me critique it on the spot, so you leave knowing exactly what to fix and why.

Why this topic matters

If you're active on LinkedIn, people will inevitably click your profile. It's basically a landing page for your professional skill set. If it sucks, you'll lose people here. Which is a missed opportunity to have people reach out to you for jobs, speaking gigs, and consulting gigs. Can we least make sure you're avoiding the common mistakes? 😅 BTW happy to critique your profile - come hang out!

Title: How I Use This Claude Skill to Grow My LinkedIn Audience

URL Source: https://www.kieranflanagan.io/p/how-i-use-this-claude-skill-to-grow

Published Time: 2026-07-24T11:06:17+00:00

Markdown Content:
Anyone building a personal audience through content has, at some point, been whacked by algorithmic changes. This is happening on LinkedIn all the time as they attempt to deal with the onslaught of AI-generated content.

The Pangram Labs study (published July 9, 2026) scanned over 1 million posts across five platforms. LinkedIn was the most AI-saturated by a wide margin: over 40% of long-form posts (250+ words) were fully AI-generated, and LinkedIn accounted for 62% of all AI-flagged content across the five platforms studied.

It’s not just LinkedIn; I stopped really investing in X when the algo update no longer rewarded the kind of content I enjoyed posting. We’ve recently seen our YouTube channel take a huge hit as the algorithm has changed to account for AI-generated videos.

And so, this month, I’ve seen a huge drop in the performance of my posts on LinkedIn, and I thought, huh, I wonder why. LinkedIn’s content analytics suck. So, I got busy and built my own dashboard featuring a new metric that I believe is the most important to track if you want to grow an audience on that platform.

_**IMPORTANT NOTE:**People over on LinkedIn pointed out you’re not allowed to use browser extensions to scrape data from LinkedIn. My recommendation is not to use the Claude skill; instead, take screenshots of your posts’ analytics. Have Claude then parse the images for the metrics cited below. Will leave Claude skill below as can be adapted for other purposes._

In this post, I’ll walk you through it, and you can download a templatized version of the dashboard and a Claude Skill to build your own version.

[See the live demo dashboard →](https://searchbrat.github.io/linkedin-dashboard/linkedin-dashboard.html)

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GiK9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4670c86e-3f23-4ef9-b982-10b6573b02be_2540x1504.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GiK9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4670c86e-3f23-4ef9-b982-10b6573b02be_2540x1504.png)

A single interactive dashboard that lives inside Claude as an Artifact you can update anytime, populated by a single Claude skill that uses Claude computer.

The interactive dashboard features:

*   Monthly trend charts for impressions, reach, followers, gained, and engagements.

*   Click any month to see an overview of performance for that month, broken out at the post level.

*   Top 10 leaderboards broken out by impressions, engagements, and virality.

*   In-network vs. out-of-network reach so you can see which posts break out of your bubble. THIS is the most important metric for LinkedIn that no one tracks. The dashboard makes it easy.

*   A 🔥 viral badge on posts where more than half the reach came from outside your network

*   Full post content you can click to expand and re-read

A living dashboard inside Claude that updates every time you run the skill.

_As per above, the following has been updated to account for the fact using Claude’s Chrome extension to gather data is against LinkedIn’s TOS._

Go to your LinkedIn analytics page. You need to capture two things for each month you want to track:

**Your post list.** Open your analytics, filter by the month, and screenshot the table showing all your posts with their impressions, engagements, and other stats. If your posts don’t fit in one screenshot, take multiple ones. Get every post.

**Individual post analytics.** For your top-performing posts, click into the detailed analytics view and screenshot the breakdown showing in-network vs out-of-network reach, followers gained, and members reached.

Don’t overthink this. If you can see the numbers on your screen, Claude can read them.

Open a new Cowork session in Claude. Upload all your screenshots and use this prompt:

> “Extract all the LinkedIn analytics data from these screenshots. For each post, capture: the post content (or first line), date published, impressions, engagements, followers gained, members reached, and in-network vs out-of-network percentage. Then build me an interactive HTML dashboard as an Artifact with monthly trend charts, a leaderboard of top posts, and month-by-month post breakdowns. Flag any post where more than 50% of reach came from outside my network as viral.”

Claude will read every number from your screenshots, structure it all into data, and build the full dashboard. The whole process takes a couple of minutes.

Next month, take fresh screenshots and open a new Cowork session. Upload them alongside your existing dashboard Artifact and say:

> “Here are my LinkedIn analytics screenshots for August 2026. Add this month’s data to my existing dashboard and rebuild it.”

Each time you do this, your dashboard grows. More months, more data, more patterns.

The reason you’d want to go back and update previous months is that content on LinkedIn has a long tail. Old posts continue to gain impressions and engagement. I’d suggest always refreshing the previous month’s screenshots when you add a new one. When I populate August 2026, I’ll also re-screenshot July’s numbers to catch the late-arriving metrics.

There is so much great analysis you can do with this dashboard, let me go through 3 great ones:

1. **In-Network vs Out-of-Network Reach:**I remember feeling like there was a similar drop in my posts performance around February. But, I wasn’t sure, until I saw this chart:

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G_8H!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbdf645fa-4b7d-48b3-9735-fc063032045b_2210x1020.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!G_8H!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbdf645fa-4b7d-48b3-9735-fc063032045b_2210x1020.png)

How much of your posts engagement are coming from within your followers (In) vs. outside (Out). The more coming from outside, the better you’ll perform. You’ll see July-26 is trending to be a poor month, similar to Feb-26. This tells me LinkedIn, for some reason, is showing my posts to less people from outside of my followers.

**2. Chat with Live Artifact**: Chat to your live artifact and gather insights about the data it’s showing you. For example, I want to know why July is performing so poorly on ‘In-Network vs. Out-of-Network” vs. June. After going back and forth it told me:

*   My last 3 posts were to ‘inside baseball’ targeting my existing followers vs. people who’d sit outside my network. I loosely agree. I do believe LinkedIn changed something 7 days ago.

*   It pulled out a couple of posts in June’26 that would appeal to a much broader audience and gave me ideas of experiments to run.

*   It said to cut the self-promotion lol. I don’t believe this is accurate, it’s because in July I referenced things I built. It marks them as self-promotion.

It’s incredibly helpful to chat about the data and gather insights. The fact all post text is added to the interactive dashboard allows you to derive real insights from writing patterns that are working vs. not working.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FkaK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a0b1da0-158f-41d8-a5b5-ff5f9083112d_2252x1284.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FkaK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9a0b1da0-158f-41d8-a5b5-ff5f9083112d_2252x1284.png)

**3. Top Leaderboards:** I love this tab, it allows you to see your top 10 posts across impressions, engagements, and virality (posts with > 50% out-of-network engagements). Add the chat feature and you can gather insights into what is working, not working and what’s changed.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y96x!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5250231-61c6-4e6b-9074-3384c6e428b4_2218x1108.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y96x!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5250231-61c6-4e6b-9074-3384c6e428b4_2218x1108.png)

The key to getting better at anything, including growing your audience on LinkedIn, starts with looking at the right data & insights.

[» Get the skill and preview the dashboard](https://github.com/searchbrat/linkedin-dashboard)

Until Next Time,

Happy AI’fying

Kieran

Marketers are building valuable things with Claude on their own, but most of that is not shared. One marketer may get dramatically more efficient, but that doesn’t mean the team does.

Instead, all that individual work piles up into sprawling, half-maintained messes across different LLMs and different [agent builders](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/where-do-agent-building-platforms-fit-in). > 
> *   The term is admittedly a bit of a shorthand, but I prefer it to “team brain” or “marketing OS” because those terms don’t capture the collaborative systems we’re really building.
> 
> *   And “Claude” here usually means Claude Code or Claude Cowork, but the ideas apply to whatever model or platform you build on.

**So I started talking to a lot of marketing leaders about multiplayer Claude and did some [prodding on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/emilykramer_who-has-a-good-workflow-for-rolling-out-claude-share-7478088670366011394-nB1D/).**

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOxU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba5e7c13-53c1-4da7-bc44-d63669ea205d_439x439.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yOxU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba5e7c13-53c1-4da7-bc44-d63669ea205d_439x439.png)

But this is kind of normal, right? **Figuring out the best way to collaborate when new tech becomes available is never easy.** Think about Slack: We’re years in and still figuring out channels versus DMs, when to thread, who to loop in. Don’t wait for team AI to be clean before you start. It’s gonna get messy and it’s okay!

> **From all of these conversations, this**_**multi-part**_**,**_**"multiplayer"**_**newsletter series took shape, to get you unstuck on building out Claude with your team.**
> 
> _Does this sound too much like a video game? Does building these systems make me feel like I’m Mario jumping through pipes and hitting brick walls in Claude Code? Yes and yes._

_We only include sponsors we’d recommend personally to our community._

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pq_s!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2bb17b28-e78e-4035-a095-c91fcefb5558_5600x1120.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pq_s!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2bb17b28-e78e-4035-a095-c91fcefb5558_5600x1120.png)

Used by Mops and Demand gen teams at Miro, Asana & Zoom.

**🔓 Offer:**[Mention MKT1](https://tractioncomplete.com/solution/marketing/?utm_campaign=27q1+mkt1+newsletter+1&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_source=mkt1) and pay nothing while they migrate and upgrade your flows.

## **In this newsletter**

**Part 1 - This newsletter:** How to get your whole team running on one Claude system

*   **[The multiplayer opportunity](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/the-multiplayer-opportunity):** Why the next AI productivity leap comes from building a shared system for your team

*   **[The 4 Cs of multiplayer Claude](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/the-4-cs-of-multiplayer-claude)** (fresh new “Kramework”): The ingredients you need to increase team productivity in Claude Chat, Cowork, and Code (or your equivalent)

*   **[Collaboration, the missing C in most AI systems](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/collaboration-the-missing-c):** What skills and setup you need to build and maintain a system that updates itself

*   **[New MKT1 MCP skills](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/we-built-you-a-shortcut-to-multiplayer-claude):** And how they can help you with all of the above

*   **[The multiplayer Claude FAQ](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/the-multiplayer-claude-faq)**: Covering what an agent actually is, what a harness is, and where your context should live

**Parts 2 and 3 - Coming soon:** How real teams are building multiplayer Claude systems, with detailed examples from Buffer, LangChain, MKT1, and more.

_Note: I wrote this for marketing teams, obviously, but it isn’t marketing-specific. **Any team building with AI together can follow this guide to building multiplayer Claude, so feel free to share more widely than usual!**_

**Your Claude system, single-player or multi-player, is incomplete without MCPs that connect Claude to functionality, context, and workflows from your tools.**We’ve invited GTM & product leaders from [Airtable](https://www.airtable.com/?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=mcp-showcase), [Attio](https://attio.com/mkt1?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=mcpshowcase_sponsorship&utm_campaign=mkt1-Y26&utm_content=July), [Framer](https://framer.link/H78Qg1G), [Mutiny](https://www.mutinyhq.com/?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=mcp-showcase), [Profound](https://www.tryprofound.com/aeo-report?utm_source=MKT1&utm_medium=sponsor&utm_campaign=mkt1_MCP_summit), [Softr](https://www.softr.io/?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=mcp-showcase), and [Zapier](https://zapier.com/?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=mcp-showcase) to show you how to use their MCP Servers live.

**Get a crash course in using Claude with these tools in 90 minutes, starting at 10 AM PT / 1 PM ET.** I’ll be hosting, and guests will be demoing real workflows and answering your questions.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y6-K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F24a626c9-f02d-4c93-9b8a-b030d05d74bf_1200x1193.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Y6-K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F24a626c9-f02d-4c93-9b8a-b030d05d74bf_1200x1193.png)

[RSVP for MCP Showcase](https://events.mkt1.co/mcp-showcase)

**Does this history with LLMs sound familiar?**

→ You started by prompting in ChatGPT

→ Then you switched to Claude and gave it real information about your company, audience, and customers to work from (which we now call context engineering). 

→ Then you added in some capabilities: a pile of skills, some MCPs, and potentially even a GitHub repo.

**Each step made AI feel more magical (and maybe more frustrating and scary too) than the last.** Prompting saved you minutes at a time. Context engineering saved you hours repeating yourself and started to fix the quality and generic-slop-output problem. Building out capabilities like skills made it possible to deliver on whole tasks, maybe even projects.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yhXU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd36a5aaa-ddfc-481b-b0d4-953b78d32c1b_600x979.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yhXU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd36a5aaa-ddfc-481b-b0d4-953b78d32c1b_600x979.png)

The next step in this evolution isn’t to just build a more robust system for yourself**. The big productivity leap will come from turning what your most AI-fluent teammates build and learn into a system the whole team runs on.**

When a team runs on shared context and shared capabilities, every improvement one person makes shows up in everyone’s next run. Nobody re-solves a problem someone already solved. Team gains start to compound really fast. Spread that shared system across your whole company, and the gains are bigger still.

That shared system includes four main parts, [what I call the 4 Cs](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/the-4-cs-of-multiplayer-claude), and the rest of this newsletter walks through each one.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ici_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F93d8521b-c59a-47ca-9847-6a8cdbfea71d_800x848.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ici_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F93d8521b-c59a-47ca-9847-6a8cdbfea71d_800x848.webp)

> #### **Don’t build a system of silos—we’ve messed this up in GTM before!**
> 
> 
> This all reminds me of a situation that I’ve been [critiquing for a while: the SDR model](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/sdr-marketer-ratio) from 3-7 years ago. 
> 
> Companies hired armies of reps to build workflows in silos (building out outbound sequences in Salesloft and Outreach). They were incentivized to hit their numbers, but never to automate what they were doing. Hires therefore had to scale linearly with revenue targets. Scaling individual behavior in silos instead of turning the best workflows and learnings into team gains is just silly. GTM engineering emerged over the last year or so partly to fix that, by taking what works from individual reps and turning it into systems. 
> 
> _Let’s not fall into the same “trap” with AI systems for teams!_

Before I talk about what it means to build a multiplayer system it’s probably worth being clear about what doesn’t count. 

**Multiplayer Claude is not…**

*   Just paying for [a team Claude plan](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/do-we-need-the-claude-team-or-enterprise-plan-for-this)

*   Dumping documents into a shared project or drive

*   Letting everyone build their own skills that never leave their laptop

*   One AI enthusiast making tools nobody else adopts

**A true multiplayer Claude system needs all four of what I appropriately call the 4 Cs:**

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZALu!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F646e4d47-6658-472b-8a20-4318b1afb051_1200x559.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZALu!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F646e4d47-6658-472b-8a20-4318b1afb051_1200x559.webp)

In this newsletter, I’ll be advocating that teams use the 3 Claudes (Chat, Cowork, and Code*) and a shared GitHub repo to build their multiplayer AI system. There are certainly other options, but for simplicity we’ll stick with those here.

_(*Another side note: why are there so many Cs in this newsletter?!)_.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!whfj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3fe640db-599a-402a-bdb6-45960252e1c2_1200x239.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!whfj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3fe640db-599a-402a-bdb6-45960252e1c2_1200x239.png)

Before I break down each C, let me give you some examples of what happens when your 4 Cs start flywheeling into a very powerful system (so you know what you’re striving for!):

*   **Your team has one living source of truth, not twelve copies:** Someone learns something new from won deal analysis using the [Attio MCP](https://attio.com/mkt1?utm_source=mkt1&utm_medium=mcpshowcase_sponsorship&utm_campaign=mkt1-Y26&utm_content=July), uses Claude to update the one canonical ICP definition everyone’s Claude references, and the whole team gets it instantly. Nobody is working from a stale copy or dated info.

*   **Someone ships a fix, everyone benefits:** The [GACCS brief](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/169687940/start-every-project-with-a-gaccs-brief) skill your teammate (let’s call them Katie) made keeps formatting the goals section wrong. You fix the skill file and push it to the team repo in GitHub. Next time anyone runs it (including people who never noticed the problem and Katie too), it’s right.

*   **Corrections don’t die in a chat session:** You tell Claude “stop using em dashes” for the tenth time. That correction belongs in the shared voice skill, that everyone’s Claude.md references, so it applies for everyone, not in a chat that ends. _(RIP em dash, I miss using you all—the—time)._

*   **Skills get used across sub-functions:** Everyone becomes more capable, more full-stack, and more of a [Gen Marketer](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/gen-marketer) because they can use the skills built by the experts and learn from them. E.g. The content marketing skills may get used by growth marketing; the product marketing skills may get used by ops.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ERZw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8332f6ad-6e63-4b7f-9d59-248b8558d46c_600x559.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ERZw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8332f6ad-6e63-4b7f-9d59-248b8558d46c_600x559.webp)

> **[Simon Heaton](https://www.linkedin.com/in/heatonsimon/), who runs growth marketing and data at [Buffer](https://buffer.com/?utm_source=mkt1),** explains how sharing skills helps marketers become generalists:
> 
> _“Our content marketer creates these great content marketing skills. There’s no reason why our growth marketer shouldn’t have access to those to **round himself out in areas where maybe he’s a little bit weaker** compared to her.”_

> My convo with Simon was really valuable (his teams’ workflows will be featured in more detail later in this series!) and **I have to give him full credit for the capabilities and context breakdown**. He used this language, I loved it, here we are:
> 
> _“There’s the [capability](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/what-counts-as-a-capability) layer, which is the executional stuff like skills, workflows, reusable prompts, reference files, the things that actually do the work. And then there’s the contextual layer, which is the knowledge base.”_

**Now I’ll explain each of the 4 Cs in more detail.**

#### **Quick start: multiplayer Claude**

1.   **Get Claude Code running** in the desktop app. [Start building skills there](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/where-should-your-team-build-skills), if you can prompt you can do this too!

2.   Tell Claude Code you want to **share skills via a GitHub and a plugin** with your team and to walk you through this (if this isn’t set up yet).

3.   **Point your claude.md file** to wherever your team context lives and to your shared team repo [where your capabilities live](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/is-a-skill-context-or-a-capability). Tell your team to do the same on their machines.

As I mentioned, getting real gains from Claude means going beyond Claude chat and getting into Cowork and Code too. Some teams use other LLMs and “[harnesses](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/what-is-a-harness)” as their home base, or [build agents that run on their own](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/so-what-is-an-agent-actually). I’m defaulting to the Claude + GitHub repo setup for this newsletter.

_More on harnesses, agent builders, etc. [in the FAQ at the bottom of this newsletter](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/i/196812313/the-multiplayer-claude-faq)._

#### Quick start: Context

1.   **Feed Claude your world, not just your strategy**. Start with your marketing strategy, then add the rest of the context Claude needs to know, including sales calls, meeting notes, launch plans, customer stories, messaging guides, and brand guides.

2.   **Connect MCPs** to get info from other tools (CRM, call recorder, calendar, docs, project management tool) so Claude always has the latest.

3.   **Codify the important stuff in one shared home**: Docs in a GitHub repo, an Obsidian vault, or Notion (but not Google Drive / Docs) so the whole team works from the same source of truth.

When using Claude Cowork or Code as your “harness,” context is everything Claude knows about your world before you ask it to do work. The easier it is for Claude to read, the more time it saves you and your team. Feeding info and data like this into LLMs has a name now: context engineering, a term Tobi Lütke popularized in mid-2025.

> **[Maja Voje](https://www.linkedin.com/in/majavoje/),** a fellow [newsletter writer](https://knowledge.gtmstrategist.com/) I often compare notes with, puts it well in her piece in [Attio’s GTM Atlas](https://atlas.attio.com/build-your-gtm-brain):
> 
> _“**Prompting is actually the worst way to use Claude**. The real unlock is context engineering: you upload your base information once, and it stays as a persistent window of context for everything that comes after.”_

For a marketing team, this starts with getting your marketing strategy into Claude. I’ve written a full guide on how and made a set of MKT1 MCP skills to help. _[Read it here: Build a marketing strategy skill in Claude Code.](https://newsletter.mkt1.co/p/build-marketing-strategy-skill-in-claude-code)_

But you can’t loading context in isn’t a one and done situation, because context changes. It has to stay current, and it has to live somewhere Claude can reach easily. _(Claude & Google Docs aren’t best friends.)_

And one warning: Most people are just trying to get Claude to connect to a million sources and they’re not making a specific source of truth. They’re just having it connect to all their tools and hoping for the best. **Codify the important stuff somewhere central, and use the data you pull in from other tools to keep it updated. hink of it as making a living knowledge base just for Claude.**

> [David Johnson-Igra](https://wearescribes.xyz/) of Scribes, who convinced me to start using [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/#utm_source=mkt1), has been building “living” context systems for his clients:
> 
> _“Everyone is pointing Claude to a bunch of static marketing files for context. **My thesis is that’s problematic** because our voices aren’t stagnant. They evolve.”_

#### Quick start: Capabilities

1.   **Build repeated tasks and workflows as skills** in Claude Code. If you can prompt, you can build a skill that does it for you.

2.   **Connect MCPs** to bring functionality and data from your other tools (CRM, analytics, website builder, AEO tool) into Claude. Use them as part of the workflows you build into your skills too.

3.   **Push every skill to your shared repo** so one person’s build reaches the whole team.

**I am using the word “capability” as an umbrella term for something you build once so Claude can do a job repeatedly.**Here’s a quick overview of what goes into this category:

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vnqM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ab1de89-80de-4fd5-a4eb-d90f1b2349ef_1200x607.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vnqM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6ab1de89-80de-4fd5-a4eb-d90f1b2349ef_1200x607.webp)

**Capabilities (and your entire multiplayer system) get a whole lot better when you layer in MCPs & APIs from the other tools you use:** This is how you connect the dots across your stack, make skills more powerful, bring more context to all of your other capabilities, etc. 

_Reminder: MCPs connect Claude to the tools where your work and data live. If there’s no official Claude Connector MCP, you can connect an API through the [Zapier MCP](https://zapier.com/templates/mcp?utm\_source=mkt1&utm\_medium=email&utm\_campaign=mcp-showcase) or directly with an API key and a wrapper._

> **🔌 To get a firsthand look at what top GTM MCPs can do, [join our MCP Showcase this Tuesday, July 28, 1-2:30pm ET ➜](https://events.mkt1.co/mcp-showcase)**

kept.heading: SPOTIFY'S 265-MILLISECOND OBSESSION (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Spotify won by making legal music feel as fast as piracy instead of competing on catalog or price. It treated speed as the product and built playback that started in about 265 milliseconds by combining local caching, prefetching, and peer-to-peer delivery. Only 8.8% of audio came from Spotify's own servers because cached files and other users handled most of the work. Find the biggest reason people choose an alternative product, then remove that friction even if it means building your product around customer expectations set by a competitor.

## **Spotify's obsession with speed**

![Image 9](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/c4c99845-d3a2-4e02-9852-404a73fe163d/Section_dividers_Final_Cut_right_to_left_transparent.gif)

![Image 10](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/f7fd7017-92c9-48b8-bcd3-89934f10196f/Chess_move_header__1_.png)

## Chess Move

**_The what:_**_A TLDR explanation of the strategy_

Blink once.

Knock a domino over.

Say the word “Spotify”.

Each of those things take _**more**_ time than it takes for Spotify to start playback of a song.

In 2009, a **Wired** writer described the Spotify beta as _"a magical version of iTunes in which you've already bought every song in the world."_

Not bought. Not downloaded. Just there, the instant you hit play.

→ That _feeling_ was the product.

**Spotify** launched in 2008 into a market that had already lost. The fastest way to get a song was to steal it, and no legal company could beat the convenience of a file downloaded straight to your hard drive, for $0.

Spotify founder Daniel Ek stopped competing with iTunes and started competing with **The Pirate Bay**, on the one important axis that piracy hadn’t quite nailed: **speed**.

The obsession was utterly total.

❝

_"We spent an insane amount of time focusing on latency, when no one cared. Because we were hell-bent on making it feel like you had all the world's music on your hard drive."_

~ Daniel Ek

They got a song to start in a median of **_265_** milliseconds, faster than most brains register a wait.

Behind-the-scenes, they assembled an engineering masterpiece, with only **_8.8%_** of the audio coming from Spotify's own servers.

The rest came from your computer’s _cache_ and, for years, from _strangers' laptops._

You read that right. Let’s learn how.

![Image 11](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/9800b2e7-05b1-4027-b05d-0cb9d898bc86/Section_dividers_Final_Cut_left_to_right_transparent.gif)

💡

**Strategy Playbook:** Speed beats free.

![Image 12](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/c4c99845-d3a2-4e02-9852-404a73fe163d/Section_dividers_Final_Cut_right_to_left_transparent.gif)

![Image 13](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/0e579e69-fb1e-440a-937e-dfbfe0525df2/Handover_Breakdown.png)

## Breakdown

**_The how:_**_The strategic playbook boiled down to 3x key takeaways_

### **1.****Spotify vs iTunes vs piracy**

Every music startup in 2008 was trying to _out-iTunes_ iTunes. That would mean a bigger catalogue, a slicker store, better price.

Spotify ignored all of it.

They noticed that the real winner in the digital music battleground was trending towards another player entirely: **_piracy_**.

And while piracy had a limitless catalogue and unbeatable price, users did have to _spend a lot of time_ hunting for safe seeders, then wait for files to download and import into their media player of choice.

![Image 14](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/d0349c0a-d128-40e9-976f-a02d45d0b526/image_1_framed.png)
Copping an ungodly amount of traffic from my IP in 2013

So Spotify built against that. A streaming engine that felt like the file was already yours.

Spotify's own product and engineering lead put it bluntly:

❝

_"One way to think about Spotify, it was just legal and fast piracy. So I really think it was about speed."_

~ Gustav Söderström

**Napster** and **LimeWire** had already trained a generation to expect all music available at their fingertips. Spotify couldn’t argue with that expectation.

So it met it → full catalogue + artist pages + playlists on top → a near-perfect playback experience.

Piracy had already written the spec for user behaviour. Spotify just had to legally build and ship it.

![Image 15](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/ef47ba17-28a4-4fbc-bd24-0534d3f472c9/image_10_framed.png)

### **2. The µTorrent hire that built the engine**

You can't obsess over milliseconds without someone who can shave them. Spotify's answer was to buy the best low-latency engineer in the world.

In 2006, they acquired **µTorrent,**the wildly popular BitTorrent client.

![Image 16](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/d9d50090-b39f-4f8a-a63f-e0b0025722a5/image_3_framed.png)
Shoutout to all the seeders out there holding it down.

They ended up selling it only months later but that actually didn’t matter.

The code was never the point.

❝

_"Spotify bought µTorrent, but what we really wanted was Ludvig Strigeus."_

~ CTO Andreas Ehn

Strigeus, µTorrent's creator, went on to build Spotify's original streaming engine, the peer-to-peer core that made instant playbacks possible, using the same family of technology that powered piracy itself.

So what exactly did he build?

### **3. How to fake instant at scale**

Instant playback is a trick of attention.

Latency is dominated by the first few 100 milliseconds, so Spotify _made the opening of a song as fast as possible_, and let the rest arrive however was cheapest.

![Image 17](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/6be8c679-268a-4999-88ea-6272eb8259d3/image_4_framed.png)

So what happens when you hit play? 4 things:

**→ Cache first.** 55.4% of the audio you heard came straight from your device's local cache. Zero network, totally instant.

_That's music you already played, still sitting on your hard drive. Spotify never deleted it after playback, so hitting a song twice isn't streaming at_ _all, it's just opening a file._

**→ A server head start.** If the track wasn't cached, Spotify streamed roughly the first 15 seconds from its own servers over an already-open connection.

_The client holds a live connection to Spotify the entire time you're logged in, so there's no dial-up ‘time to get connected’ moment when you hit play. The request goes down a pipe that's already active, and it only asks for the opening_ _seconds, not the whole file._

**→ Peers for the bulk.** While that intro played, your client pulled the rest of the song from other users who already had it, 35.8% of all data (those strangers' laptops).

_You only need the first 15 seconds urgently. The remaining 3 minutes have minutes to show up, so Spotify handed that job to strangers to save themselves_ _the bandwidth bill._

**→ Pre-fetch the next track.** Before the current one ends, Spotify loads the next song, so "hit next" is gapless too.

_In the closing seconds of the current song, Spotify quietly pulls the opening of whatever's up next into your cache, so by the time you press_ _skip it's already ready to play._

Throw these together and you have a ~265ms median start, with <1% of plays stuttering, and only 8.8% of bytes served by Spotify itself.

![Image 18](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/512c2273-da7e-4a90-b9a2-710d64c098f1/image_5_framed.png)

And when 265 milliseconds still wasn't instant enough (the average human brain can detect down to ~200ms), Ek admitted the last fix was psychological:

❝

_"We never got it down to 200 milliseconds consistently... but when you play with things such as the throbber, and you actually cognitively make it move even before there's sound, the human brain perceives it to be instant even though technically it wasn't."_

~ Daniel Ek

![Image 19](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/9800b2e7-05b1-4027-b05d-0cb9d898bc86/Section_dividers_Final_Cut_left_to_right_transparent.gif)

![Image 20](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/1ed892b2-25fd-4647-8573-c63fc62b1e23/Handover_file__2_.png)

## Rabbit Hole

**_The where:_**_3x high-signal resources to learn more_

[![Image 21](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/c06aea80-4fed-4261-ad75-e4de03fef004/image_7_framed.png)](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/spotify-architecture-pressing-play/12578378?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)

### **[Spotify: Large Scale, Low Latency, P2P Music-on-Demand Streaming ↗](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/spotify-architecture-pressing-play/12578378?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)**

##### **[30 minute read]**

One of the denser reads, but well worth it.

2 Spotify engineers show their working: how half your music came from other people's laptops and you never noticed.

Shows exactly where the 265ms median actually comes from, how the cache → server → peer split measured, and why only 8.8% of bytes ever touched Spotify's servers

[![Image 22](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/cc87cf1a-0a94-42b6-b0a6-23cb67aa5930/image_8_framed.png)](https://mastersofscale.com/daniel-ek-how-to-build-trust-fast/?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)

### **[Daniel Ek on Masters of Scale ↗](https://mastersofscale.com/daniel-ek-how-to-build-trust-fast/?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)**

##### **[35 minute listen]**

Reid Hoffman gets Ek to confess the 200ms miss, and how a moving loading bar covered for it.

→ Why they obsessed over latency when no one asked

→ The throbber trick, in Ek's own words

→ Building trust when the product has to feel instant

_35 minutes on why perception is a product surface._

[![Image 23](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/2b6825e0-ce9d-4611-a41b-70aeb5976dea/image_9_framed.png)](https://www.acquired.fm/episodes/spotify-ceo-daniel-ek?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)

### **[Acquired: Spotify CEO Daniel Ek, The Complete History and Strategy ↗](https://www.acquired.fm/episodes/spotify-ceo-daniel-ek?utm_campaign=spotify-s-265-millisecond-obsession&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=strategybreakdowns.com)**

##### **[1hr 38min listen]**

Recorded at Spotify HQ, Ek walks the whole arc from racing pirates to running the audio internet. The definitive origin deep-dive, the business behind the milliseconds.

_3 hours wasn’t enough._

kept.heading: GOOGLE DOESN'T PUNISH AI CONTENT; IT PUNISHES BAD CONTENT (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google doesn't penalize AI content. It rewards quality. Fully AI pages can rank in top positions, but most high-ranking results are still largely human-written. Higher AI use trends with lower rankings, indexing rates, and impressions, though there's no strict cutoff. Many high-AI pages are still indexed, and performance remains stable over time. The real issue is quality, as scaled, low-value content tends to underperform regardless of whether AI was used.
