Title: Jasper vs. ChatGPT: Which is better? [2026]

URL Source: https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/

Published Time: June 3, 2024

Markdown Content:
At first glance, [Jasper](https://www.jasper.ai/) and [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/) seem similar—they're both [generative AI tools](https://zapier.com/blog/generative-ai-tools) that can create content in a split second. But there's a big difference here: ChatGPT is an [AI chatbot](https://zapier.com/blog/best-ai-chatbot/) that's flexible enough to handle just about any task you throw at it, while Jasper is a specialized [AI marketing tool](https://zapier.com/blog/best-ai-marketing-tools/).

I've spent countless hours using both apps in my personal and professional life. For example, I used Jasper to help me [scale content production](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-ai/) for my previously niche website. And I've been using [ChatGPT](https://zapier.com/blog/how-does-chatgpt-work/) to take care of other time-consuming tasks in my work.

There have been major upgrades to both apps since I first started using them, so I dug into each one again to see how their features stack up. Here's what I discovered when I compared Jasper AI vs. ChatGPT.

**Table of contents:**

*   [Jasper AI vs. ChatGPT at a glance](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#glance)

*   [Both use state-of-the-art models](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#ai-models)

*   [ChatGPT is simpler; Jasper provides more guidance](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#ease-of-use)

*   [Both offer customization features; Jasper's are easier to use and more in-depth](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#customization)

*   [ChatGPT has more generalized functionality; Jasper is better for marketing tasks](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#generalized-functionality)

*   [Both offer agentic AI, but Jasper's is more marketing-focused](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#agentic)

*   [ChatGPT is more affordable](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#pricing)

*   [Jasper AI vs. ChatGPT: Which should you use?](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-chatgpt/#which)

## Jasper AI vs. ChatGPT at a glance

If you want a quick breakdown of both tools, here are my observations:

*   **ChatGPT** is more versatile and better for generalized AI assistance.

*   **Jasper** is built for marketing teams and is better for creating marketing content.

*   You'll get more out of ChatGPT if you already know [how to write an effective prompt](https://zapier.com/blog/gpt-prompt/); Jasper provides prompt assistance along the way.

|  | **Jasper** | **ChatGPT** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ideal user** | Marketing teams looking to generate, refine, and improve marketing materials | Users looking for an AI assistant to handle complex or time-consuming tasks of any nature |
| **Models** | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Powered by Jasper's proprietary model and other AI models, including OpenAI's GPT models | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Uses OpenAI's state-of-the-art models |
| **User experience** | ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Easy to use, but has lots of options and features, so it can be more confusing | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Super easy to use with a chat-style interface for interactive content generation |
| **SEO capabilities** | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Offers SEO content templates and connects with Surfer SEO for content optimization | ⭐⭐ Can optimize content based on specific prompts but isn't as seamless as Jasper |
| **Integrations** | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Integrates with third-party marketing tools, including Zapier | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Supports custom GPTs and integrations with Zapier |
| **Pricing** | ⭐⭐ No free plan and quite expensive for small businesses | ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Free plan available; paid plans start at $8/month |

## Both use state-of-the-art models

Like ChatGPT, Jasper is powered by OpenAI, but it also pulls in the power of other [LLMs](https://zapier.com/blog/best-llm/) (large language models), like the ones from [Google](https://zapier.com/blog/google-gemini/), [Anthropic](https://zapier.com/blog/claude-ai/), and Cohere—as well as [its own proprietary models](https://developers.jasper.ai/docs/the-jasper-ai-engine). Jasper's AI engine then decides the best combination of models to use for each prompt, which, in theory, should deliver high-quality outputs.

ChatGPT uses [its state-of-the-art models](https://zapier.com/blog/openai-models/), which are usually the most advanced ones available. If you're on a paid plan, you can manually choose which model ChatGPT runs on or let ChatGPT automatically pick one, optimizing for quality and speed.

At this point, all the AI models in play are incredibly impressive, so you're unlikely to detect any significant difference in content quality.

## ChatGPT is simpler; Jasper offers more guidance

When it comes to ease of use, you can't go wrong with either [ChatGPT](https://zapier.com/blog/how-to-use-chatgpt/) or Jasper.

Once you log in to ChatGPT, you're met with a clean, intuitive interface—one with limited bells and whistles to navigate through. Just type your prompt, and you're off.

![Image 1: New ChatGPT conversation](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/dzDP5i9Ot2Hk35IIQyKtH/03e90abfa9a1b26a4d5fdc9c4d7da3e7/image6.png)

Jasper used to require more fiddling to get started with, but it recently had a facelift that makes it look eerily like ChatGPT. Design inspiration aside, that means you can now dive into prompting right from your dashboard on Jasper too.

![Image 2: Jasper's dashboard, where you can start a chat](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/3vxk2cLGSPj6HfHGR07sOu/916622c848ece74ee51e4e4eeea348fd/image9.png)

Prompting Jasper from your dashboard will launch Jasper Chat or a Jasper AI agent, depending on your prompt. Unlike ChatGPT, though, Jasper provides additional support to help you write a strong prompt. For starters, there's the _Enhance prompt_ button that helps with refining your prompt and providing additional context.

![Image 3: The Enhance prompt option in Jasper](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/yaLikFVEZEosAdcEenQfS/fee49a870ae767f5c8203dfdd1770026/image2.png)

There's also Jasper's [prompt library](https://www.jasper.ai/prompts) that's filled with over 500 content generation prompts, grouped by use case. All you have to do is copy and paste the prompt into your Jasper chat.

Additionally, you can start generating content by choosing from over 100 Agent workflows (essentially templates) that run the marketing gamut, from email campaigns to product descriptions to blog articles.

![Image 4: Jasper's library of apps (templates)](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/56syuSpuxJNFxLPB7O0BJR/e79b4fad895fe99e78876f064f7f91f9/image4.png)

These are thoughtfully designed to help you create specific content types for different marketing functions. Each includes prompts to guide you on the type of detail to provide so the agent can understand the tone and context of the content you want to create. For example, if you want to create a Facebook post, you'll input your brand voice, audience, key message, preferred length, and CTA to ensure you get targeted output.

![Image 5: Setting up a Facebook post on Jasper using an app](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/1acX5YlRbFDL6Z0L3iDqps/1bf7ca04d7046d7b876776bc310a9b05/image8.png)

At the end of the day, both apps require some level of [prompt engineering](https://zapier.com/blog/prompt-engineering/). And it may take some trial and error to get the content up to snuff. If you have less experience writing effective prompts, Jasper's step-by-step assistance may be a welcome addition. But if you've got your prompting down to a science, ChatGPT offers a faster way to get to the final results.

## Both offer customization features; Jasper's are easier to use and more in-depth

Jasper and ChatGPT allow you to customize the AI so that it can tailor its outputs to suit your needs.

For all ChatGPT users, you can [use custom instructions](https://zapier.com/blog/how-to-train-chatgpt-on-your-own-data/#custom-instructions)—a feature that lets you add background information about yourself or your business and specify how it should respond. This way, you don't have to keep providing the same context or directives.

![Image 6: Custom instructions popup in ChatGPT.](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/wKo71Ua9pt6ev6Ybk6OxA/45fdd88b63b3b227b768c554285814d4/image3.png)

Alternatively, you can use _Projects_, a way to keep related chats, memories, custom instructions, and other reference material in neatly contained groups. This way, you can jump between projects and have ChatGPT simultaneously context switch with you.

For ChatGPT users on paid tiers, you can [build your own custom ChatGPT](https://zapier.com/blog/custom-chatgpt/) (called GPTs). They operate similarly to custom instructions, but with a few key differences: you can create multiple custom GPTs and upload knowledge sources to each one. This way, you can easily toggle between chatbots to get the right kind of AI-powered support for the occasion. You can also set up your GPT to perform actions outside ChatGPT.

![Image 7: OpenAI's GPT builder with an example GPT](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/5MvScIHbpOybKq39Wzhjr2/de503168b7169f39bd3128bb9d9e1596/image10.png)

Jasper, on the other hand, allows you to create or upload extensive branding documentation, including brand voice, audiences, your knowledge base, style guide, and visual guidelines. And this is super quick to do by choosing _Jasper IQ_ in the left-hand sidebar.

![Image 8: Popup in Jasper with the option to import content to train Jasper to write in your voice. ](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/3gzzWw8JOKD3XPKTrPXAFh/46fb34d9e0ff1919f0679f1c0a972905/image1.png)

If you don't have these documents formalized yet, you can give Jasper a handful of links to your existing content (minimum 1,000 words), and it'll generate a brand voice for you, which you can both edit and test before saving. I particularly love the testing feature. It generates two samples of content (based on your given prompt) side-by-side, one _with_ and one _without_ your brand voice applied, so you can see the difference super clearly.

If you _do_ have these documents prepped already, you can simply upload them directly to Jasper IQ—or connect them via Google Drive integration. With the latter option, Jasper stays up to date automatically when you make changes to any of your documents within Google Drive.

Either way, you can add multiple brand voices and designate each for different types of content. For example, you can save a more authoritative voice for your blog and a cheekier version for social.

If all you want is to [train your chatbot to write like you](https://zapier.com/blog/train-chatgpt-to-write-like-you/), Jasper will get you there faster and more accurately.

## ChatGPT has more generalized functionality; Jasper is better for marketing tasks

Content marketing goes beyond writing emails, blog posts, and social media captions. You also have to research, create graphics to accompany your posts, share drafts with your team for review, run performance reports, and analyze how well your content is (or isn't) performing—just to name a few.

ChatGPT can natively help with almost all of the above (for anything it can't, there's a [Zapier](http://zapier.com/) integration for that). For example, using [ChatGPT Deep Research](https://zapier.com/blog/chatgpt-deep-research/) and its ability to search the web, you can research any topic to find thorough, documented, and clearly cited information from diverse online sources in minutes.

![Image 9: The Deep Research options in ChatGPT](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/60lUfE3AfwcTbzi9P1MbJ0/9473d80210659a87f4bce0eebbffdb28/image5.png)

You can also upload a spreadsheet of, say, last quarter's email analytics and ask questions about it. Or upload, say, a PDF of your guide to basic dog training and have ChatGPT convert it into a presentation for your next dog training webinar. Or you can use it to generate AI images of your product in the wild to create a truly scroll-stopping social post.Or connect your CRM and ask ChatGPT questions about your leads. And this is just scratching the surface of all that you can do, beyond generating text, with ChatGPT alone.

Jasper can also generate AI images and analyze data. But in terms of data analysis, it's hyper-focused on giving you only content-related insights. It also doesn't include video generation.

But Jasper's focus on marketing tasks can be a huge boon. Its Agents help less-seasoned marketers create content that will resonate. Plus, Jasper integrates with other tools that fit seamlessly into marketing workflows. For example, when you connect Surfer SEO to Jasper, you get ranking data for the article you're writing, so you can keep search engine visibility in mind without hopping between tools.

## Both offer agentic AI, but Jasper's is more marketing-focused

The chat experience in Jasper acts as a gateway to AI agents that work across pre-built flows to draft campaigns, build outreach sequences, and generate specific content types with less manual, back-and-forth prompting. Or you can create custom agents via Jasper Studio, or browse the Agent Library, which includes over 100 pre-built AI agents.

Jasper also offers powerful orchestration features via Grid's spreadsheet-style interface, which makes generating content at scale as easy as clicking "Run all." You can set up a workflow to create dozens of variations, campaign assets, or content pieces in one batch.

![Image 10: Jasper's Grid feature](https://images.ctfassets.net/lzny33ho1g45/4jiwGQvOevZ77pKVdvECLE/58a2345a3bce7213c057e55feacdc552/image11.png)

ChatGPT also supports Agent Mode, but it's more individual and session-based than Jasper's persistent agents—able to perform one-off, request-based tasks, rather than performing autonomous, ongoing work. The recently launched Workspace Agents (powered by Codex) is more like Jasper's orchestration, but it's only available to Business and Enterprise users as of this writing.

But if you live in ChatGPT, you can install [Zapier MCP](https://zapier.com/mcp), and your AI gets access to 9,000+ apps—Gmail, Slack, Salesforce, HubSpot, Calendly, and thousands more—directly from the chat window. Instead of switching between tools to create a doc, check some data, or update a record, you just ask. Zapier handles the action, and your credentials stay out of the model entirely, so there are no API keys pasted into prompts.

Note that Jasper is one of those 9,000+ apps. That means you can connect it to the rest of your workflow through Zapier—triggering Jasper content generation from a form submission, a CRM event, a spreadsheet row, or straight from your AI chat window, and routing the output wherever it needs to go.

Either way, Zapier gives you one governed connection across every AI tool you use. Add an app once, revoke access from one place, and every workflow that depends on it updates automatically.

## ChatGPT is more affordable

If you're looking for a [free AI tool](https://zapier.com/blog/free-ai-tools/), ChatGPT is a good place to start. There's an $8/month [ChatGPT Go](https://zapier.com/blog/chatgpt-go/) plan, and e ven if you upgrade to [ChatGPT Plus](https://zapier.com/blog/chatgpt-plus/) for $20/month to access advanced features, it's well worth the price point.

Jasper doesn't offer a free plan. Instead, it offers a seven-day free trial with paid plans starting at $59/seat/month (billed annually). To access more advanced features like uploading unlimited knowledge sources, custom AI agents, full access to Grid, and team collaboration—the ones that truly help you scale content production—you'll need to pay for a custom Business plan.

So if budget matters to you, ChatGPT is the way to go.

## Jasper AI vs. ChatGPT: Which should you use?

Jasper and ChatGPT are powerful tools in their own right—and either can assist you with your content creation workflows. Ultimately, your choice will depend on the _kind_ of AI assistance you're looking for. Here's what it boils down to:

*   **Jasper** is the better option if you're looking to generate marketing-specific content.

*   **ChatGPT** is the better option if you need a more generalized tool that's flexible enough to handle varied tasks.

One thing I can't emphasize enough, though, is that no matter which tool you use, you'll need to spend time fine-tuning your prompting skills to get the best results.

**Related reading**:

*   [Jasper vs. Copy.ai: Which AI writing tool is better?](https://zapier.com/blog/jasper-vs-copy-ai/)

*   [The best AI writing generators](https://zapier.com/blog/best-ai-writing-generator/)

*   [Writesonic vs. Jasper: Which AI writing tool is best?](https://zapier.com/blog/writesonic-vs-jasper/)

*   [Perplexity vs. ChatGPT: Which is better?](https://zapier.com/blog/perplexity-vs-chatgpt)

*   [The best ChatGPT alternatives](https://zapier.com/blog/chatgpt-alternatives)

*   [What are Claude computer use and OpenAI Operator?](https://zapier.com/blog/claude-computer-use-openai-operator)

_This article was originally published in June 2024 and has also had contributions from Jessica Lau and Kiera Abbamonte. The most recent update was in July 2026._

Title: AI Is Not Replacing Marketing. It’s Crowding the Room.

URL Source: https://almund6ef.substack.com/p/ai-is-not-replacing-marketing-its

Published Time: 2026-07-28T08:02:32+00:00

Markdown Content:
Hi, I’m Ara. Welcome to AI with Ara, a growing community for curious minds, builders, and professionals who want practical AI insights without the noise.

Every issue brings the latest AI tools, trends, simple tutorials, and real workflows you can use right away. Clear, useful, and easy to follow, so you can learn faster, work smarter, and stay ahead.

**[Sign up for free](https://almund6ef.substack.com/).** Get smarter. Get confident. Grow with AI.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!J9TL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dc24330-354d-4fdf-87e2-f667c3ecf098_498x373.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!J9TL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dc24330-354d-4fdf-87e2-f667c3ecf098_498x373.gif)

Marketers keep asking which channel AI will kill next.

Will websites disappear? Will search collapse? Will email finally die?

Probably not.

Technology changes quickly, but human habits change slowly. AI is reshaping search, just as social media changed news and streaming changed television. Yet new channels rarely erase older ones.

They change their role.

Radio survived television. Websites survived social media. Search continues even as more people use AI tools.

The better question is not, “What dies next?” It is, “What role does each channel play now?”

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QKe9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3ead41e2-8c09-48d3-bcfe-dd7d713d453c_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QKe9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3ead41e2-8c09-48d3-bcfe-dd7d713d453c_836x471.jpeg)

Marketing loves declaring things dead. Television, radio, SEO, websites, email, and organic social have all received the funeral treatment.

These predictions fail because people do not change their habits like software. Adoption depends on age, income, trust, work, convenience, and confidence.

Some people adopt new platforms immediately. Others continue using familiar channels because they still work.

New behavior usually adds another path rather than removing the old one.

Look at television.

Some adults have never tuned a television through an antenna. To them, television means Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, TikTok or any other video available on demand.

Others still organize their viewing around free-to-air television, scheduled programs and familiar newsreaders, without needing multiple subscriptions, passwords or software updates.

They live in the same year but follow very different media habits. In 2025, ACMA found that 91% of Australian adults used an online video service during an average week. Yet 52% still watched traditional free-to-air television, excluding catch-up services. That figure even rose slightly after years of decline.

Streaming transformed the market, but it did not eliminate television. It created a more fragmented viewing landscape.

Marketers often mistake adoption for extinction. In reality, new channels usually divide attention.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vx24!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9774633-6c7a-401e-a6f3-85f6525719bc_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vx24!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb9774633-6c7a-401e-a6f3-85f6525719bc_836x471.jpeg)

Streaming music and podcasts have changed how Americans listen, but traditional radio still commands significant attention. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Americans spent 61% of their daily ad-supported audio time with radio. Podcasts accounted for 21%, streaming music for 15% and satellite radio for 3%. The channels now serve different purposes:

*   Radio often supports commuting, local information and passive listening.

*   Podcasts offer depth, expertise and personality.

*   Streaming music provides control and personalization.

*   Social video supports discovery and cultural relevance.

New formats often push older channels toward the situations where they remain most useful.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!N6nE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae72cb5e-b7ea-4ebb-8227-d0306c0245da_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!N6nE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae72cb5e-b7ea-4ebb-8227-d0306c0245da_836x471.jpeg)

News consumption may be the clearest example of the entire problem.

The University of Canberra’s _Digital News Report: Australia 2025_ found that television remained the most popular main source of news at 37%. However, for the first time in the eleven-year history of the Australian survey, social media overtook online news websites as a main source.

Social media accounted for 26%, while online news websites accounted for 23%.

Television still leads, social media is growing, and news websites remain important. At the same time, people also get information from creators, podcasts, group chats, screenshots, rage-bait headlines and that one uncle who treats Facebook comments like research.

There is no single path anymore. One person watches the evening news, another scrolls TikTok, while someone else visits a publication directly or learns about the story through a screenshot from a friend.

Audiences build their own mix of trusted and convenient sources.

AI adoption is substantial and growing.

In February 2026, 49% of U.S. adults said they used AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Copilot, up from 33% in 2024.

However, adoption varies by age. Adults under 50 were roughly twice as likely as older adults to use ChatGPT.

Customers are not abandoning Google, websites, email, and social media at the same speed. Some will ask AI, while others search, read Reddit, watch reviews, open emails, or ask friends.

Many will use several channels before making a decision. The marketer’s job is to understand how those behaviors connect.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h_Ix!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe5b4e53-306d-4038-a16c-ae652f693991_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!h_Ix!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe5b4e53-306d-4038-a16c-ae652f693991_836x471.jpeg)

AI may reduce traffic to generic informational pages, but it does not remove the need for websites. Customers still need a place to:

*   Verify what the business offers.

*   Review pricing, products and availability.

*   Examine evidence, reviews and case studies.

*   Compare options and answer detailed questions.

*   Contact the company or complete a purchase.

Search also remains a major discovery channel. Google held 86.67% of the U.S. search engine market in June 2026, while Bing held 8.73%.

At the same time, AI is becoming an additional referral source. Adobe Analytics data from May 2026 found that U.S. shoppers arriving through large language models spent more time on retail websites and generated more revenue per visit than visitors from non-AI sources.

Notice where those shoppers still went to compare products and complete their purchases: the retailer’s website.

AI may change discovery. Websites still handle depth, trust, and conversion.

So where should marketers focus?

*   The real problem is not that marketing channels are disappearing. It is that marketing teams are expected to manage too many of them.

*   A modern team may be responsible for search, paid advertising, social media, email, YouTube, TikTok, LinkedIn, influencers, public relations, podcasts, review platforms, partnerships, AI assistants, events and offline campaigns.

*   Then someone asks why the team has not tested everything.

*   Doing everything is not a strategy. It is panic wearing a lanyard.

*   The better approach is to define the job of each channel and invest according to the audience, business model and customer journey.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vhU4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59752d98-4fa4-4d0f-b3a5-2284c2305a52_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!vhU4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F59752d98-4fa4-4d0f-b3a5-2284c2305a52_836x471.jpeg)

The question should not be, “Which channel wins?” It should be, “What role does each channel play?” Once channels are organized by their purpose rather than their popularity, the marketing environment becomes easier to understand.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yxj0!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f497e7d-c0f7-4c97-bf61-d06db04b6f45_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yxj0!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f497e7d-c0f7-4c97-bf61-d06db04b6f45_836x471.jpeg)

A website remains one of the few assets a business controls.

Algorithms change, social reach falls, ad costs rise, and AI may summarize content without sending traffic. A strong website still controls the message, provides proof, captures demand, and guides customers toward action. It needs clear pages, useful content, fast performance, and simple conversion paths.

Honestly, good riddance.

Customers discover brands through search, AI, social media, video, creators, PR and partnerships. These channels should support one another. One strong article can rank in search, earn AI citations, become social content and support a video, email or sales conversation. The goal is not more content. It is better content that works across channels.

Wild concept, I know.

Attention is easier to earn than trust. Trust comes from evidence, clear explanations, real examples and a distinct point of view. As AI makes generic content easier to produce, credible expertise becomes more valuable. Brands that show their work and support their claims will stand out.

Retention includes email, CRM, remarketing, support and lifecycle communication. Existing customers and leads have already shown interest. Useful reminders, relevant offers and timely follow-ups can create more value than constantly chasing new attention. As acquisition becomes harder, retention matters more.

No one knows exactly how AI, search and customer behavior will change. That makes adaptation more valuable than prediction.

Teams need customer research, testing, creative iteration and practical measurement. The goal is not to chase every platform, but to identify meaningful change early. The strongest brands will be the ones that learn fastest.

Long-term planning is harder because AI, search, privacy rules, customer expectations and measurement systems are changing quickly.

Yet people still want convenience, answers, reassurance and proof. They compare options, ask friends and often buy emotionally before justifying the decision. Businesses should focus on:

*   Strong owned assets.

*   Clear positioning.

*   Useful content.

*   Search, social and AI visibility.

*   Reliable email and CRM.

*   Regular research and measurement.

Marketers used to think primarily in channels. Now they need to think in behaviors.

Instead of asking, “Should we be on TikTok?” ask whether the audience uses short-form video to discover, validate or understand products within the category.

Instead of asking, “Is SEO dead?” ask how customers look for answers, compare options and develop enough confidence to make a purchase.

Instead of asking, “Will AI kill websites?” ask how AI systems understand, summarize and recommend the brand, as well as what customers experience when they eventually arrive.

Instead of asking, “Should we send more emails?” ask what customers genuinely need to hear after showing interest. Channels are containers. Behavior is the real subject.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oij2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28643d47-fa4d-4840-a3ad-4202ad66f500_836x471.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oij2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28643d47-fa4d-4840-a3ad-4202ad66f500_836x471.jpeg)

Traditional channels often survive by taking on new roles.

*   Radio supports commuting and local information. Television supports live sports and routine viewing. Websites provide proof and conversions. Search becomes one answer engine among several.

*   Social media combines discovery, entertainment, news and commerce. AI adds another way to search, compare and decide. AI is not replacing the marketing system. It is joining it.

Focus on what remains valuable when channels change.

Build assets the business controls, create useful information, invest in trust and strengthen retention. Test new behaviors without abandoning proven fundamentals.

One customer may ask ChatGPT, while another searches Google, watches YouTube, reads Reddit, opens an email or asks a friend.

The goal is not to predict one winning channel. It is to build a marketing system that works across the full journey. Technology moves through releases. Humans move through habits.

Phew! That was a lot, right? But hey, knowledge is power🌟. We hope this edition gave you some insights and maybe even cleared up a few doubts.

kept.heading: THE ‘DEAD INTERNET THEORY' IS REAL. AND IT'S KILLING THE WEB AS WE KNOW IT (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The 30-year-old online advertising model was never really selling attention, it was selling access to a human being who could be flattered or worn down into a purchase. Agents don't have that vulnerability, so surveilling one produces nothing to sell, and more than half of all web traffic is now agents rather than people. What a business can still offer an agent is qualification on merits like price, reliability, and data quality, not persuasion, which is a fundamentally different kind of customer relationship to build for. The model isn't being reformed by regulation or backlash, it's dying because the traffic itself changed completely.

kept.heading: GOOGLE'S AI SEARCH IS RAPIDLY BECOMING THE DEFAULT, NEW DATA SHOWS (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI Overviews jumped from 15% to 43% of Google searches in a year, while AI Mode visits more than doubled to 279 million by May.
kept.article_text:
Title: Google’s AI search is rapidly becoming the default, new data shows

URL Source: https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/27/googles-ai-search-is-rapidly-becoming-the-default-new-data-shows/

Published Time: 2026-07-27T15:57:12+00:00

Markdown Content:
AI search is rapidly becoming the default, whether users like it or not. In just a year’s time, Google’s AI-generated answers in search, known as [AI Overviews](https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/23/googles-ai-overviews-have-2b-monthly-users-ai-mode-100m-in-the-us-and-india/), have gone from appearing in 15% of searches to 43%, according to a new report, driving a shift in how web users consume information online.

In a [recent analysis](https://www.similarweb.com/corp/the-2026-generative-ai-landscape/) of the generative landscape, market intelligence firm [Similarweb](https://www.similarweb.com/) noted that what began as an AI layer on top of search has become an integral part of the search journey itself, as Google drops users into AI Overviews, where they can then continue their research via Google’s more conversational [AI Mode](https://techcrunch.com/2025/05/20/googles-ai-mode-rolls-out-to-us-will-add-support-for-deeper-research-comparison-shopping-and-more/).

![Image 1](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/similarweb-at-11.03.08-AM.jpg?w=680)

**Image Credits:**Similarweb

During the same period, AI Mode visits rose from 126 million in June 2025 to 279 million by May 2026.

The data illustrates a broader [change in how users search](https://techcrunch.com/2026/05/19/google-search-as-you-know-it-is-over/) the web — a shift from an era when Google provided a simple list of blue links to click through and read to one in which Google itself is the destination, sourcing its answers and information from the websites it indexes.

This, in turn, appears to increase the time users spend on Google’s platform rather than using it only as a tool to discover websites. Over the past year, Similarweb’s data shows that the average length of Google searches has risen, suggesting that people are now replacing their short keyword-based search queries with longer, more natural conversational ones designed for AI.

![Image 2](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/similarweb-at-11.04.28-AM.jpg?w=680)

**Image Credits:**Similarweb

This change has not been welcomed by publishers, who are [losing out on referral traffic](https://techcrunch.com/2025/06/10/googles-ai-overviews-are-killing-traffic-for-publishers/) due to the rise of AI citations that don’t lead to clicks. Last year, Similarweb [reported](https://techcrunch.com/2025/06/10/googles-ai-overviews-are-killing-traffic-for-publishers/) on this trend, noting in particular how devastating it was for news publishers. More recently, tech infrastructure company Cloudflare [introduced tools](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/01/cloudflares-new-policy-pushes-ai-companies-to-pay-for-publishers-content/) that allow publishers to fight back by [blocking AI crawlers](https://techcrunch.com/2024/07/03/cloudflare-launches-a-tool-to-combat-ai-bots/) from their websites unless those AI companies pay for access to their content through [its marketplace](https://techcrunch.com/2025/07/01/cloudflare-launches-a-marketplace-that-lets-websites-charge-ai-bots-for-scraping/).

While AI citations don’t always lead to users clicking through to a destination, the number of AI responses that include a citation has risen more than fivefold during the past year, Similarweb’s new report says.

Still, just 6.8% of U.S. ChatGPT desktop queries included citations as of May 2026, despite this growth. (Some industries fare better, with travel, retail, and sports queries generating cited responses more frequently than others.)

![Image 3](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/similarweb-at-11.15.18-AM.jpg?w=680)

**Image Credits:**Similarweb

There is some hope for publishers, however. In terms of ChatGPT at least, U.S. desktop referrals have improved after a May 7 search update, which saw the proportion of visits landing on webpages more than double from 25% in March 2026 to nearly 60% by May 30, 2026.

This suggests that users are taking advantage of the more prominent blue links within AI-driven search results when they’re available.

![Image 4](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/similarweb-at-11.18.51-AM.jpg?w=680)

**Image Credits:**Similarweb

Even with these improvements, the larger AI search trend remains unchanged, as Google transforms itself from a gateway to the wider web into a destination in its own right.

kept.heading: INFLUENCER MARKETING DIDN'T BLOW UP, FIVE YEARS OF DEAL DATA SHOWS IT MATURED INSTEAD (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: A newly released report based on five years of influencer deal data shows that influencer marketing has matured into a more structured and efficient channel. Average creator contract values grew from $3,065 in 2019 to $7,400 in 2025 while average deal timelines fell 36% as contracts and campaign processes became more standardized. Brands get better results from long-term creator relationships because 24% of partnerships now include repeat engagements, and repeated campaigns build audience trust over time. Micro-creators often generate stronger revenue per follower while larger creators still deliver greater overall reach.
kept.article_text:
Title: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years Of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead

URL Source: https://www.netinfluencer.com/influencer-marketing-didnt-blow-up-five-years-of-deal-data-shows-it-matured-instead/

Published Time: 2026-07-29T08:12:27-04:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](https://www.netinfluencer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-20260729_102928-af10ac.png)
Influencer Marketing has been called the “Wild West” of digital advertising long enough to become a conference-panel reflex. A new data study from [G&B Digital Management](https://www.gb-dm.com/) and [Bobbie](https://www.thebobbieagency.com/), drawing on five years of G&B’s proprietary deal records, makes the numerical case that the description no longer fits.

The study is the work of [Kyle Hjelmeseth](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kylehjelmeseth/), founder and CEO of G&B Digital Management, and [Monica Caponigro](https://www.linkedin.com/in/monicakhattar/), Founding Managing Director of Influencer Marketing agency Bobbie. Kyle founded G&B in Los Angeles in 2015 and has built it into a 120+ creator roster executing more than 3,000 brand partnerships annually across lifestyle, fashion, beauty, and food. Monica, who previously led Nordstrom’s Creator Center of Excellence and served as SVP of Digital Influencer Strategy at Hunter, founded Bobbie in 2025. The New York agency focuses on creator and Influencer Marketing programs for brands ranging from startups to major retailers.

“We’re tired of hearing it’s the ‘Wild West’ of marketing,” Kyle says. “We’ve been here creating the foundation of this place.”

Their report, “Taming the Wild West: The New Laws of Creator ROI,” argues that Influencer Marketing did not blow up overnight. It grew through three measurable structural shifts: rising contract values, compressing deal timelines, and a growing share of repeat brand-creator relationships.

For Kyle, releasing G&B’s proprietary deal data publicly was a deliberate act. He believes talent management firms holding this data have an obligation to share it. “I don’t think anybody from a talent management firm has released its data,” he says. “That would be, kind of, a first.”

HEADSHOTS

## **From $2,500 to $50,000 for the Same Post**

The most direct evidence of change, Monica argues, is what pricing looked like a decade ago. Two creators with equivalent follower counts could quote wildly different rates to the same brand with no shared rationale. “One person might have come to us and said, ‘I’ll charge you twenty-five hundred,’ and then the exact same basically equivalent creator would have been like, ‘I’ll charge you fifty thousand,'” she says. “There really just were no rules and benchmarking because it didn’t exist.”

Kyle describes early brand behavior as “throwing spaghetti against the wall.” His first managed creators would receive outreach spanning luxury labels and fast-fashion retailers in the same week, with no apparent targeting logic. Some brands demanded granular performance data upfront; others sent $50 and some product samples with no stated objective. Both approaches coexisted because there was no shared standard for what a deal was supposed to accomplish or cost.

The report’s primary dataset shows average creator contract values growing from $3,065 in 2019 to $7,400 in 2025, which the report characterizes as approximately 95% growth over five years. Monica’s first instinct was to attribute the increase partly to inflation. She quickly complicated that read. “The deals are getting more complex,” she says. “There’s more value, and the results speak for themselves.”

![Image 2: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](blob:http://localhost/0c765ada43744c6aa54b334e5c248206)
Kyle argues the numbers also serve a legitimizing function for the industry. “It’s not crazy to go from three thousand to seven thousand,” he says. “If you’re doing what you’re supposed to be doing, you’re sowing back into your communities, you’re growing.” Growth in contract values was not confined to a single vertical. Technology brands posted the highest five-year compound annual growth rate in the dataset at 18.2%, while entertainment came in lowest at 10.0%. All categories moved in the same direction.

![Image 3: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](blob:http://localhost/0c765ada43744c6aa54b334e5c248206)
## **What Compressed Deal Timelines by Nearly 40%**

Between 2021 and 2024, the average time from contract signing to content completion fell from 80.75 days to 51.56 days, a 36% reduction. Kyle identifies several compounding factors. With more than 80% of G&B’s deal flow coming through agencies, contract language has standardized to the point where most agreements read from similar templates. “Most contracts are pretty standard as far as what they’re looking for,” he says. “The time it takes to redline and move through contracts has dropped a millionfold since I first started.”

![Image 4: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](blob:http://localhost/0c765ada43744c6aa54b334e5c248206)
Creator-side professionalism has developed in parallel. Creators who have been in the industry for several years now arrive at campaigns with workflow systems, milestone awareness, and faster turnaround than their predecessors.

Monica identifies repeat partnerships as a structural driver the data captures indirectly. When a brand and a creator have already executed two or three campaigns together, the legal terms are largely settled, the brief is shorter, and the creator’s familiarity with the brand’s voice narrows the revision cycle. “If I’ve worked with one of Kyle’s talents five times before,” she says, “that agreement is going to take us a matter of minutes.”

Deal activity in the G&B dataset grew from 1,800 completed partnerships in 2020 to 3,100 in 2024. Kyle attributes much of that volume increase to efficiency gains compounding at the mid-tier level, a segment he argues is the most active in the entire Creator Economy and the most underreported.

## **One in Four Partnerships Repeats, and Kyle Is Done With the Word ‘Test’**

The report finds that 24% of brand-creator relationships in the G&B dataset include multiple engagements. Monica reads that number as evidence of progress and as a remaining gap. “One in four partnerships are now repeat,” she says. “But that also leaves three in four that are not.” She notes the jump in repeat partnerships from 2023 to 2024 was larger than earlier year-over-year changes, which she takes as evidence that longer-term programming is gaining structural adoption.

![Image 5: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](blob:http://localhost/0c765ada43744c6aa54b334e5c248206)
Kyle’s objection to prevailing industry practice goes beyond the data. He argues that framing a first deal as a “test” is not a neutral description of an initial campaign. “I would go on the record and say that I think the term ‘test’ is offensive,” he says. “Do you want to test for your job?” In his experience, test framing rarely comes with shared performance targets and frequently precedes ghosting or below-market rates, a structural disincentive built into the language of the pitch before any content is produced. His prescription: enter a first deal with explicit alignment on what a successful outcome needs to show to earn a second.

Monica frames the case for repetition in terms of what the data shows about audience behavior. A first post introduces a brand to a creator’s followers. A third or fourth activation is where sustained belief forms. “By that last point,” she says, “you really genuinely believe that the creator uses the product.”

## **Mega Creators Earn More. Smaller Ones Earn More Per Follower.**

A 2025 snapshot of 94 G&B creators shows a predictable top-line pattern: mega creators with more than one million followers averaged $473,000 in brand-partnership revenue, compared to $291,000 for macro creators, $148,000 for mid-tier, and $116,000 for micro creators. The less obvious finding is that revenue per follower runs in the opposite direction, with smaller tiers generating more efficient returns on a per-audience basis.

![Image 6: Influencer Marketing Didn’t Blow Up, Five Years of Deal Data Shows It Matured Instead](blob:http://localhost/0c765ada43744c6aa54b334e5c248206)
Monica draws on her time at Nordstrom to illustrate the point. Some micro-level creators with modest followings drove six-figure sales outcomes for the retailer. “You would never have thought,” she says, “but they drove like six-figure sales for Nordstrom.” Her practical takeaway is that brands should match creator tier to campaign objective rather than defaulting to reach. Kyle adds a counterpoint about unpredictability: a creator who does not regularly post about a particular category can generate outsized purchase intent from a single relevant post because her audience engages that day. “You can’t discount macros, mid micros, whatever, because they can surprise you,” he says.

The ability to be surprised, in Kyle’s view, is not a measurement failure. It is part of the channel’s value, and no amount of benchmarking data can fully eliminate it.

## **Execution Is the New Competitive Advantage**

The report’s concluding argument is that access to creators is no longer a differentiator. Discovery tools are widely available, pricing has standardized, and practically every brand at scale now runs influencer programs. “Now just about every single brand in the world is doing Influencer Marketing,” Monica says. “So it comes down to the brands that are doing it right, really well.”

She defines that standard as maintaining the quality of briefing, vetting, and creator relationship management even as timelines compress. Speeding up the process without cutting those fundamentals is, in her view, the actual execution challenge. “We’re executing Influencer Marketing at speed, but we’re not compromising quality,” she says. Both Kyle and Monica identify the human element as the variable most at risk as AI tools enter influencer workflows. Their shared position is that automation should accelerate process, not replace relationship management.

Monica hopes the current period will be defined by brands learning that technology and human judgment are not substitutes. “I hope the data shows this was the moment brands realized that, as AI became more embedded in marketing and decision-making, the human element became more valuable, not less,” she says in written responses following the interview. Kyle frames the same period in structural terms. “The entire creator space has officially professionalized,” he says. “This moment will be remembered as the tipping point, the year the Creator Economy truly grew up.”

_Image source: G&B, Bobbie_ _The full report is available_[_here_](https://www.gb-dm.com/bobbie-gb-study-2026)
