Title: Why DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats Integrated LLMs Into Search Three Different Ways

URL Source: https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/why-doordash-instacart-and-uber-eats

Published Time: 2026-07-28T15:30:42+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bFVc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F27c61630-38d1-481d-9639-a65b8b426b5c_1200x620.png)](https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_072826Headline)

Users expect apps and agents to reach the tools they already work in. Every integration that gets you there is a different OAuth flow, a different token lifecycle, weeks of infrastructure before you write a line of product code.

[WorkOS Pipes handles it with one API call.](https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_072826Pipes) Pre-built connectors for GitHub, Slack, Salesforce, Google Drive, and more. Pipes handles OAuth, token refresh, and credential storage. You call the real provider API with a fresh token, every time.

Over the last few years, three of the biggest food delivery companies rebuilt their search systems around LLMs. DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats were solving the same problem of trying to understand a user’s intent when they type something in search. They were also accessing more or less the same research base. And yet, the architectures they shipped look quite different from each other.

That divergence is one of the most interesting aspects of modern development using LLMs. Once we understand why each company landed where it did, we will have a mental model for thinking about how AI can be integrated into any production system.

Adding an LLM to an existing stack comes down to one question: how deeply should the LLM reach into the runtime?

Ultimately, DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats each answered that question differently, and the specific LLM each chose was secondary. The specific model each company picked was secondary. The infrastructure they already had in place is what determined the answer.

In this article, we will walk through their differing solutions and try to make sense of their choices and understand the pattern behind them.

_Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References are present at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies._

Type “something healthy for a rainy evening” into a food delivery app and watch what comes back. The result we get today is somewhere between useful and impressive. The same query five years ago might have returned a random jumble of items, because keyword search treats the words as a bag of tokens rather than as an intent, and the query offers little for keyword matching.

This pattern repeats across several common failure modes in food search. For example:

*   **Synonyms:** “Soda” and “soft drink” describe the same product, but a keyword engine treats them as different tokens.

*   **Typos:** “Mozzarela” should retrieve mozzarella results, but the spelling mismatch breaks the lookup.

*   **Shorthand:** “Gf pizza” meaning gluten-free pizza requires the system to recognize an abbreviation as a synonym for the full phrase.

*   **Language mix:** The Spanish word “pan” means bread, while the English word “pan” means a cooking vessel, so a bilingual search bar has to disambiguate.

*   **Word-sense ambiguity:** “Apple” the fruit and “Apple” the company share the same spelling but mean different things, and the right answer depends on context.

Each one is a potential moment where the user’s intent and the catalog’s words fail to line up.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wq55!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd73dbb14-f3cd-466e-b1d2-4dda97a2a29f_3004x1820.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wq55!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd73dbb14-f3cd-466e-b1d2-4dda97a2a29f_3004x1820.png)

Two harder problems lie beneath this:

*   **The long tail:** Grocery and restaurant platforms see an enormous number of unique queries. Any specialized model trained on conversion data struggles with queries that appear only a handful of times, because rare queries are rare by definition.

*   **The constraint problem:** A query like “vegan chicken sandwich” has a hard constraint inside it, and similarity-based retrieval might return a chicken sandwich that violates the constraint, because the similarity score still looks close. Dietary restrictions, allergens, and quantity filters all sit in this bucket.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cXcN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6bc7b7fa-c5bc-4122-a978-834863b9a323_2306x1504.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cXcN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6bc7b7fa-c5bc-4122-a978-834863b9a323_2306x1504.png)

Food search is the right domain to watch this play out, because all of these failure modes show up at the same time. In the subsequent sections, we look at how different companies handled these situations differently.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!o5VA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50857283-5449-47f7-9475-120119a8d02d_1600x840.png)](https://go.bytebytego.com/Spacelift_072826)

How do platform engineers keep pace with a growing development team at a $2B AI company? Join Lawrence Aiello, Platform Engineering Lead at Rogo, on August 11 to learn how his team evaluated and implemented a modern IaC platform. He’ll cover:

*   The evaluation criteria that mattered when Rogo picked a modern IaC platform, evaluating solutions like **Pulumi, OpenTofu, Crossplane and more**

*   What “it just works” looks like in practice for infrastructure operations

*   Why a reliable platform is the foundation for AI-driven infrastructure workflows

If your infrastructure platform has become another system to maintain, this session is for you.

[Register Now →](https://go.bytebytego.com/Spacelift_072826)

DoorDash already had a knowledge graph for items and restaurants when LLMs became viable for production. The graph held structured attributes for every item, including dish type, dietary preference, cuisine, brand, and flavor.

Their approach was to use LLMs to enrich this graph offline by extracting attributes from SKU data, and to use LLMs at runtime only for parsing queries into chunks that could link back to the graph. Retrieval itself stayed keyword and graph-driven.

Consider the query “small no-milk vanilla ice cream.” The LLM segments it into three chunks.

*   “small” is a quantity attribute.

*   “no-milk” is a dietary preference attribute that maps to the canonical label “dairy-free.”

*   “vanilla ice cream” splits further into a dish type (”ice cream”) and a flavor (”vanilla”).

Each chunk is then linked to a specific field in the knowledge graph. The dietary preference becomes a hard filter, so only dairy-free items get retrieved. The flavor becomes a soft preference for ranking. The dish type narrows the candidate pool.

See the diagram below:

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GLos!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c8da434-96a8-4f4a-b824-fb88d9f9d8ea_3310x1950.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GLos!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c8da434-96a8-4f4a-b824-fb88d9f9d8ea_3310x1950.png)

What distinguishes DoorDash’s approach is how they constrain the LLM’s outputs.

They use retrieval-augmented generation as a guardrail rather than as a generator. For each query segment, an approximate nearest neighbor lookup retrieves the top 100 closest taxonomy concepts from the existing graph. The LLM is then prompted to pick from that list rather than invent labels. This is a clever inversion of the usual RAG pattern, where RAG typically injects context into a generator. Here, RAG defines the entire output space, so the system only ever produces concepts that the rest of the design already knows how to handle.

The measured impact is a roughly 30% lift in the trigger rate for popular dish carousels, all delivered through an architecture whose runtime stays mostly classical.

The takeaway is that DoorDash’s LLM lives mostly offline, mostly in batch, working on the periphery of the runtime.

When Instacart’s engineers first investigated an off-the-shelf LLM to categorize the search query “protein,” the model returned chicken, tofu, beef, and other high-protein foods.

The answer is reasonable by any reading of the English language. The problem is that Instacart’s actual users, when they type “protein,” are looking for protein bars and protein powders. The model’s general world knowledge and the company’s specific user behavior were pulling in different directions, and this small failure points at the central problem Instacart had to solve.

The system they were replacing was complex.

Query category classification ran on a FastText model, query rewrites came from a separate engine that mined session behavior, and spell correction, query tagging, and aisle classification each ran as a separate model with its own data pipeline and serving infrastructure. The maintenance burden was substantial, and tail queries still suffered because each model needed its own labeled data, and labels for rare queries are scarce by definition.

Instacart’s strategy is layered across three approaches:

*   **Context engineering:** Retrieval-augmented generation pulls Instacart-specific context (top-converted categories, historical conversion data, catalog details) into the prompt before the LLM sees a query.

*   **Post-processing guardrails:** Semantic similarity filters drop LLM outputs that drift away from the original query.

*   **Fine-tuning:** For the most advanced tasks, the team fine-tunes Llama-3-8B on Instacart’s proprietary data, so domain knowledge gets baked directly into the model weights.

See the diagram below:

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zhNd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba6ea2d7-2aa6-4ccb-91de-6a5e8af5e8af_3322x1854.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zhNd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba6ea2d7-2aa6-4ccb-91de-6a5e8af5e8af_3322x1854.png)

The serving architecture splits along the head-versus-tail distribution.

Head queries hit an offline RAG-and-cache pipeline that is latency-tolerant and deeply context-engineered, while tail queries hit a real-time fine-tuned Llama-3-8B model that keeps latency under 300ms through adapter merging, H100 GPUs, and autoscaling.

The cache serves queries the company has seen before, while the real-time fine-tuned model serves everything else, which is where the cold-start tail lives. This split is exactly the kind of decision the head-versus-tail traffic distribution encourages, since pre-computing only pays off for queries that repeat.

After this solution, query rewrite coverage jumped from 50% to over 95%, with 90%+ precision across substitutes, broader rewrites, and synonyms. The real-time fine-tuned model improved search quality for the bottom 2% of queries (the cold-start tail), cutting scroll depth by 6% and complaints about poor tail-query results by half.

The takeaway is that Instacart’s LLMs live at the query understanding layer, with some offline-cached and some online and fine-tuned, while retrieval and ranking downstream are still done by traditional machine learning and information retrieval systems. The LLM brain is doing the upstream interpretation, while the classical approach is doing the downstream serving.

Uber Eats faced the same problem the others did, plus a complication. They run across multiple verticals, including restaurants, grocery, and retail, across multiple markets, and across a long list of languages.

Their previous setup was fragmented, with separate BERT-based embedding models per vertical, lexical search in places, and the operational overhead of maintaining all of these in parallel. The goal was a single retrieval system that handled every vertical, every market, and every language with one consistent embedding space.

The architecture they decided on is a classic two-tower setup, where a query encoder and a document encoder each produce vectors in a shared space, and matching is done by similarity in that space.

The twist is in what sits inside each tower, because both towers use a fine-tuned Qwen LLM as their backbone embedding layer. The query tower runs online, embedding each incoming query in real time, while the document tower runs offline and pre-embeds billions of documents into an HNSW vector index (a graph-based structure built for fast similarity search at scale). This split is what makes the system economically possible, since running a heavyweight LLM on every document at query time would be prohibitive, while pre-computing once and looking up at retrieval time is tractable.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RCUZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F01484d48-9e8a-4b91-97aa-baf2fc71e1b5_2878x2212.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RCUZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F01484d48-9e8a-4b91-97aa-baf2fc71e1b5_2878x2212.png)

The fine-tuning matters as much as the architecture choice.

Out of the box, Qwen brings world knowledge and cross-lingual capability, which is what handles the Spanish “pan” problem mentioned earlier. Fine-tuning on Uber’s proprietary query-document interactions teaches the embedding space what Uber Eats users actually care about, and this is what gives the system its domain alignment. The base model contributes general semantics, and the fine-tuning adds the specific rules of Uber Eats.

What makes the system viable at scale is a stack of optimizations:

*   Matryoshka Representation Learning trains a single model whose embedding can be truncated to different lengths, and Uber serves at 256 dimensions in production with under 0.3% recall loss compared to the full 1,536.

*   Scalar quantization (int7 instead of float32) cuts latency in half again.

*   Pre-filters on hexagon, city, and fulfillment type shrink the candidate set before the ANN search even runs.

The numbers tell the cost story. Tuning the ANN parameter k dropped latency by 34% and CPU by 17% with negligible recall impact, quantization halved latency at recall above 0.95, and MRL cut storage by nearly 50%. Together, these are the engineering choices that let a fine-tuned LLM serve as the retrieval substrate of a production search system at Uber Eats’ scale.

The takeaway is that Uber Eats’ LLM is the embedding model itself, since every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector, and retrieval at every level depends on LLM-produced representations.

If we line up the three companies on a single axis labeled “how deeply does the LLM sit in the runtime,” the pattern provides some insight.

*   DoorDash sits on the left, with the LLM enriching the catalog offline and parsing queries with constrained outputs while the runtime stays mostly classical.

*   Instacart sits in the middle, with LLMs handling query understanding through offline RAG for the head queries and a fine-tuned Llama-3-8B for the tail, while retrieval downstream is still traditional.

*   Uber Eats sits on the right, with a fine-tuned Qwen as the embedding backbone running for every query and pre-baked into every document vector.

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K9Kf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc449d68f-f60d-4aa6-9128-905b03a52fe2_2162x1458.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K9Kf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc449d68f-f60d-4aa6-9128-905b03a52fe2_2162x1458.png)

Each company’s position on the spectrum was largely determined by the infrastructure it already had.

*   DoorDash already had a knowledge graph that classical retrieval could exploit, so the cheapest gain came from making the graph richer and teaching queries how to talk to it.

*   Instacart had specialized query-understanding models that were hard to maintain, so the biggest win came from consolidation under a unified LLM strategy.

*   Uber Eats already had two-tower embedding infrastructure running per vertical, so the natural next step was swapping in a fine-tuned LLM as the shared backbone, allowing one model to handle every vertical and every language.

The lesson would be that before asking which LLM to use for some task, the better question is where in an existing stack an LLM would actually help.

Three of the largest food delivery companies rebuilt search around LLMs in the same window of time, with overlapping research literature and similar production constraints, and they arrived at three completely distinct architectures.

The reason food search was a good place to investigate this is that it breaks classical keyword retrieval in many ways simultaneously. Subjective queries (something healthy for a rainy evening), long-tail traffic, multilingual catalogs, and compound constraints all sit in the same search bar.

The three approaches each represent a different setting:

*   DoorDash uses LLMs offline to enrich a knowledge graph, while classical retrieval still drives the runtime.

*   Instacart uses LLMs at the query understanding layer, with fine-tuned smaller models handling tail queries in the hot path.

*   Uber Eats fine-tuned a Qwen LLM into the embedding backbone of two-tower retrieval, so every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector.

Each company’s position on this spectrum traces back to the infrastructure it already had, which is why the depth-of-integration question matters more than the model choice.

Three universal tradeoffs survived every architecture.

*   Hybrid systems are the default everywhere. Classical retrieval, knowledge graphs, and ANN indexes still do most of the work.

*   World knowledge from a pre-trained model is just a head start. Domain context still has to be injected somewhere, through RAG, fine-tuning, or both.

*   Guardrails are an important part of every production LLM system. Constrained vocabularies, similarity filters, and taxonomy enforcement quietly determine whether outputs stay aligned with the catalog.

**References:**

*   [Evolution and Scale of Uber’s Delivery Search Platform](https://www.uber.com/blog/evolution-and-scale-of-ubers-delivery-search-platform/)

*   [Scaling Multilingual Semantic Search in Uber Eats Delivery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06586)

*   [How DoorDash leverages LLMs for better search retrieval](https://careersatdoordash.com/blog/how-doordash-leverages-llms-for-better-search-retrieval/)

*   [Building DoorDash’s product knowledge graph with large language models](https://careersatdoordash.com/blog/building-doordashs-product-knowledge-graph-with-large-language-models/)

*   [Building The Intent Engine: How Instacart is Revamping Query Understanding with LLMs](https://www.instacart.com/company/tech-innovation/building-the-intent-engine-how-instacart-is-revamping-query-understanding-with-llms)

*   [Supercharging Discovery in Search with LLMs](https://tech.instacart.com/supercharging-discovery-in-search-with-llms-556c585d4720)

kept.heading: PRODUCTS ‘MADE BY MISTAKE' SELL MORE (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Accidental product flaws can become a marketing asset when a brand presents them as unique instead of hiding them. Across seven experiments, people were 27.3% more likely to buy a product with an accidental flaw and were willing to pay up to 71.8% more in some cases. This approach works best for established brands that sell products for enjoyment rather than function because uniqueness increases appeal in those categories. Pairing the mistake with a clear explanation and a limited-time promotion can help turn excess inventory into higher demand.

Title: Products ‘made by mistake’ sell more

URL Source: https://app.sciencesays.com/p/products-made-by-mistake-sell-more

Published Time: 2026-07-28T10:22:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
🎓 _**New to**_[Science Says](https://sciencesays.com/?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=insight&utm_campaign=introcta)_**?**_ _This is a 3-min practical summary of a scientific study_📩[Subscribe for $0](https://sciencesays.com/?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=insight&utm_campaign=introcta)_to get one weekly, or join the_📈[paid version](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=products-made-by-mistake-sell-more)_for 300+ insights, real-life case studies, and the exclusive_ _**Playbook of Brand Names**_ _._

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/97e8fbb3-d1d1-4a5d-80da-8379c18f3375/image.png?t=1784880535)](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=welcome&utm_campaign=email-3)

The Science Says newsletter keeps you up to date, and I hope you’re loving it 💜

If you’re a marketing pro, we built the [Science Says Platform](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=welcome&utm_campaign=email-3)to be the place you turn to before any project to check “What is the latest evidence I should know about, so I get the best possible results?”

You’ll find all our 300+ insights, like:

*   [Discount coupons: when to give % off vs $ amount off](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/coupons-when-to-give-10-off-vs-10)

*   [When to use vouchers vs free gifts for promotions](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/when-to-use-vouchers-vs-free-gifts-for-promotions)

*   [Make your discounts a bit harder to get](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/make-your-discounts-a-bit-harder-to-get)

Only paid [Platform members](https://www.sciencesays.com/join-platform?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=welcome&utm_campaign=email-3)can access them all 24/7, along with real-world case studies, the exclusive playbook of brand names, and direct access to our team of PhDs and me to answer your questions.

#### 📝**Context**

**Topic**: Product | Messaging & Copy

**For**: B2C

**Research date**: August 2017

**Universities**: New York University, Boston University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

You’re an ecommerce manager selling modern travel accessories, and you’ve noticed your latest batch of luggage tags has the wrong color mix (pink and blue instead of your signature orange and blue).

That was an expensive order and people will realize the products are not in your signature colors.

Science says you should own your mistake, and even lean into it.

#### 📈**Recommendation**

If you make mistakes in your product production (e.g. a misprint), don’t hide them. Highlight them and clearly communicate what the mistake was. Avoid this if you're new on the market or if your product is bought for its functionality (e.g. a deodorant).

People will see your product as more unique and be more likely to buy and willing to pay more for it.

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/4b27ea04-e1f5-4d5f-b725-9e68b147fcb6/Insight__336__1_.png?t=1784880753)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   People prefer, want and pay more for products with mistakes.

*   Across 7 experiments and an analysis of 3,114 eBay auction sales, scientists found that people:

    *   Paid more for artistic photos from the same seller on eBay when they had mistakes (e.g. fingers in the frame)

    *   Wanted a chocolate bar with an accidentally (vs intentionally) enriched flavor 26% more often

    *   Were 27.3% more likely to buy and willing to pay 71.8% more for an artist’s painting with an accidental mark (e.g. with a fingerprint)

    *   Were 18.8% more likely to buy, and 18.7% more interested in listening to a song with an unplanned sound addition (e.g. singer’s breathing)

    *   Were 10.3% more likely to say they would order a lasagna dish with an ingredient mistakenly added to the sauce (e.g. accidentally using nutmeg instead of pepper)

*   The effect:

    *   Works even if the mistake makes the product worse (e.g a mark on a drawing)

    *   Works regardless of scarcity (e.g. whether 100 or 10,000 are produced)

    *   Disappears if the product is bought for its functionality (e.g. a supplement) instead of pleasure (e.g. a cookie)

    *   Disappears if the manufacturer is new in business

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   We see a product made by mistake as out of the ordinary and unusual, regardless of whether it’s for the worse or better.

*   This makes us see them as [unique, making us more attracted](https://doi.org/10.1086/657163?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=products-made-by-mistake-sell-more) to them.

*   However, we think beginners are more likely to make mistakes, which makes us see their mistaken product as less unique and interesting.

*   Similarly, uniqueness becomes less relevant when we are buying for a product’s functionality.

_Want to advertise to 30,000+ Science Says readers here?_[Click here](https://advertise.sciencesays.com/?utm_source=ariyh&utm_medium=insight&utm_campaign=secondary&_bhlid=84ecf8ac2de826fa65104d41b763abbac0d17c9b)_._

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   The study didn’t look at what happens when the consequences of the mistakes are unpleasant (e.g. make the product unusable, bad smell), and where the boundary is.

*   The effect might not apply to expensive luxury items (e.g. watch, perfume, whiskey) with a mistake as it might make people concerned about the quality. However, this wasn’t tested.

*   It’s likely that overusing this tactic will backfire and reflect negatively on the brand’s image.

#### 👀**Real-life example**

Artist Colette is a brand selling work-themed hair accessories (e.g. a calendar hairclip). They announced a misprint on their calculator claw clips on social media.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/f8e81a45-0a2b-46c4-9ce8-2dbe3bc33e21/336_example.png?t=1784099353)

❌**Issue:**They posted a viral video on TikTok addressing the misprint and offering refunds or replacements to all their customers.

✅**Solution:**The mistake could have been a great opportunity to increase sales of that product stock if handled differently:

*   They could have clearly communicated the mistake but framed it as a fun, unique product instead.

*   They could have also run a limited-time offer, stopping it when the remaining stock sold out. [This limited, but justified timeframe](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/limited-time-promos-are-weaker-online) could have made it more effective.

*   Since it’s a small business and the founder is the face of the brand, she could have taken the chance to thank people for their understanding by including a [handwritten thank you note](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/handwritten-notes) in the order, boosting future sales.

#### **🔍 Study type**

Lab and online experiments, field experiment (144 train station passersbys evaluating a recently formulated chocolate) and market observation (3,114 photos sold in eBay auction sales from the same seller over 3 months in 2016)

#### 📖**Research**

#### 🏫**Researchers**

*   [Taly Reich](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ydyGFbYAAAAJ&hl=en&utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=products-made-by-mistake-sell-more). New York University

In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=products-made-by-mistake-sell-more)_). It may also not be generalizable to your situation. If it’s a risky change, always test it on a small scale before rolling it out widely._

kept.heading: WHAT ACTUALLY DRIVES INBOUND JOB LEADS ON LINKEDIN (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Data-backed analysis of LinkedIn inbound leads showing how engagement and profile optimization attract recruiters and hiring managers.
kept.article_text:
Title: What Actually Drives Inbound Job Leads on LinkedIn

URL Source: https://www.juliedx.com/insights/blog/what-drives-inbound-job-leads-on-linkedin

Published Time: 2026-07-27

Markdown Content:
[The other half Can recruiters find you? Your posts are the push, getting you into the feeds of people who can hire you. Being findable is the pull. See whether your profile shows up when recruiters search. Check your findability→](https://www.juliedx.com/job-search)
In the last six months, 70 recruiters and hiring managers have reached out to me about roles. I didn't apply to a single one of them. Thirteen were high quality, meaning real roles at the right level, location, and pay, at companies that seemed interesting.

I started the year with about 3,500 followers. I had never done organic content on LinkedIn before, and my background is mostly consumer and B2B2C marketing, not audience building. LinkedIn has never been part of any job I've held. The skills that produced this are the same ones I use at work: think about your audience, what they care about, and what would make them act. Then I audited all of it against LinkedIn's raw data exports. Here's what I found.

## Why inbound leads are the KPI

My goals on LinkedIn are personal brand, networking at scale, and right now, landing my next role. But this doesn't end when the search does. I plan to keep it running in my next job, so that the next time I'm laid off or stuck somewhere bad, the exit is smoother. I'm aware that it gets harder with age, not easier. Also it's sad that I have to say that I could be laid off again… it hasn't ever happened before until this year, but it just seems to be the norm now, and I don't want to be blindsided.

This isn't job hopping. I've stayed about five years at three of my companies, and I'd happily do it again. What I want is career security, which in 2026 means the right people knowing how you think before you need them to. Career security is yours, not your employer's. It can be done primarily by having a strong personal brand and network.

Inbound leads are the only number that measures that. Impressions measure how far content travels. Followers measure accumulation. An inbound lead, a real recruiter or hiring manager writing to you first about a real role, measures whether the right people know who you are and act on it. High quality leads matter most, medium next. Everything else is a proxy.

The KPI is already outperforming the alternative. Inbound conversations have put me in five late stage interview processes. A hundred forty-eight applications (including having advocates in my network) produced three. Same person, same resume, same market.

## How I audited it

I pulled LinkedIn's native monthly analytics exports, January through July: 151 posts, with the post text verified against LinkedIn's own URLs. Then I logged every lead with its real first-contact date, checked against my actual inbox, and rated each one for quality. Correlations across seven months are directional, not proof, and I treat them that way.

## Where the 70 actually came from

After the audit, I did one more pass: I went lead by lead through all 70 and traced how each person found me. It was the most useful hour of the whole project, because the leads split into two channels that behave nothing alike.

The recruiters come through search. About half my leads are recruiters, and almost none of them could be traced to a post. What my data does show is that reach and engagement climb together with my search appearances, and recruiters live in search. They're querying titles and skills, my profile ranks, they reach out. This channel is high volume and noisy on quality, because a recruiter often contacts you before the role is fully scoped. You can't aim it. You can only feed it.

The other half

The posting and the profile work together.

Profile optimization is the other half of getting found. See how findable your profile actually is.

[Check your findability→](https://www.juliedx.com/job-search)

The hiring managers come through content. Every single lead who mentioned my posts, ten of them now, was a hiring manager, founder, or decision-maker. Zero were recruiters. A teaching post is a work sample, and shows the value in how you think.

And there's a third channel I almost missed: the network. A quarter of my highest-quality leads came from people who thought of me because I'm visible. A friend's referral. A chain of introductions that started with someone who follows my posts. I never deliberately worked this channel. It produced some of my furthest processes.

So the two dials from the audit turn out to power different funnels. Impressions feed the search channel and lead volume. Engagement rate feeds the content channel and lead quality. And visibility overall seeds the network channel, which is nearly free.

## What held up

Engagement rate is the quality dial. One month brought 332,000 impressions and nothing came of it. My best engagement-rate month brought five of the thirteen high-quality leads. The pattern held all six months: quality leads arrive when content resonates, not just when it travels. Impressions still matter, but as surface area. Reach without resonance produced my emptiest months.

Against my baseline, where 23% of posts clear 10,000 impressions, a handful of levers kept beating it.

*   Posts with a call to action hit 10K at 44% versus 18% without, and roughly doubled engagement rate.
*   Posts written to the reader, heavy on "you," hit at 50% versus 21%.
*   Teaching posts, ones giving the reader something to do today, hit at double the rate of my personal stories.
*   A link in the body ran 41% versus 22% and had the strongest engagement effect of anything I measured, so no, links don't kill reach.
*   The 1,500 to 2,200 character range hit at 39% versus 17%.
*   A real number near the top, doing real work. Posts that open with a stake-carrying number hit at 45% versus 22%. I think because it's making it less abstract and it feels more reachable (but that's just my gut.)
*   And days where I posted once beat days where I posted more than once, two to one.

That last one is the most common self-inflicted wound I see. Yet still, sometimes I have too much to say, so I still post more than once… but that's on me.

## What didn't matter

Sounding vulnerable, sounding honest, and telling career stories all tested flat. Posts flagged for dysfunction language, transparency phrases, or employer-name storytelling performed no better than posts without them. What moved things was giving the reader something, not showing them something about me. This was actually very surprising to me, because previously I believed the opposite. I do still think being genuine is critical, but that's not really something my analysis could easily measure.

My industry content underreaches. Healthcare posts, my actual profession, hit 10K at 19% versus 29% for everything else. I keep writing them anyway, because the audience they do reach is the one that hires me. That's a KPI decision: a post can lose on reach and win on leads.

## Why none of the 70 have converted yet

I'm still in active processes, so "yet" is doing honest work. But the pattern behind the number is useful if you're expecting inbound to be a shortcut. People often reach out before they know what they're hiring for. Sometimes the level is wrong. Sometimes there's a hard non-negotiable I can't clear, like owning a seven-figure paid media budget or being in an office 2.5 hours from my house. Sometimes the pay isn't reasonable. And sometimes I get deep into a process and they choose someone else.

None of that is a failure of the channel. Five late rounds (inbound) against three (outbound), from a fraction of the effort, is the whole argument. Also, quality has been improving and I would prefer to write content than tailor resumes and apply cold to jobs literally any day of the week. It is a better use of my time. In general the leads are better, more interested, and more looking for someone like me than applying cold.

## Okay, so here's what you were waiting for. How can you do it too?

Think of this as a funnel, because it is one. You pick the number at the bottom, you learn which signal predicts it, and then every post is a top-of-funnel decision that either feeds it or doesn't. And now that I know there are three channels, every post gets a job before I write it: feed the search rank, convert a hiring manager, or stay visible to my network. In order:

*   **Start by tracking the right number.** Keep a simple log of every recruiter or hiring manager who writes to you first: who, company, date, and a quality rating you assign honestly. When you get on the call, ask how they found you. That one question is the only reliable attribution you'll ever get, because almost nobody mentions a post unprompted. Everything below exists to move this log, nothing else.
*   **Watch your engagement rate, not your impressions.** Engagements divided by impressions, tracked monthly. My quality leads arrived in my high-engagement months, not my high-reach months, and the month that taught me this had 332,000 impressions and produced nothing. For reference, my lead months cleared 2%. Yours will have its own line, but you can't see it if you're staring at reach.
*   **Teach something the reader can do today.** My teaching posts cleared 10,000 impressions at double the rate of my personal stories. The reason this works for job leads specifically: a teaching post is a work sample. A hiring manager who learns something from you has already watched you do the job. Reflection posts ask people to care about you. Teaching posts prove you're useful, which is the thing they're hiring.
*   **Write it to "you," not about "me."** Posts heavy on second person hit 10K at 50% for me, against a 21% baseline. People read to the end when the post is about them. They skim when it's about you. Before publishing, count how many sentences start with "I" and flip half of them.
*   **Open with a real number that carries the stakes.** 45% versus 22% on my data. I think it works because a number makes the post concrete before the reader decides whether to expand it (that's my gut, not the data). It has to be a real number, though. Round it, don't invent it.
*   **End with one specific ask.** Posts with a call to action hit 10K at 44% versus 18%, and roughly doubled engagement rate, which makes it the rare lever that moves both dials. Never close on a bare "thoughts?" Ask something only this post could ask, aimed at the exact person you want in your comments. Comments are where leads introduce themselves.
*   **Name real companies, tools, and numbers.** Specific beats clever. "A health plan" is forgettable. The real name is proof you were in the room.
*   **Respect the mechanics: 1,500 to 2,200 characters, one post a day, links are fine.** The length band hit at 39% versus 17%, long enough to teach and short enough to finish. My solo-post days beat my multi-post days two to one, because a second post competes with your first. And a link in the body ran 41% versus 22% with the strongest engagement effect of anything I measured, so put the link where the reader is. "Links kill reach" wasn't true on my account.
*   **Give every post a channel before you write it.** Broad teaching posts are search-rank fuel: judge them on reach and engagement, not leads. Craft posts in your actual domain are hiring-manager magnets: judge them on who shows up, not impressions. And a periodic what-I'm-working-on post keeps the network channel warm. When a post is allowed to fail at the two jobs it wasn't given, you stop killing your best content for missing the wrong number.
*   **Write for the people who hire you, even when it costs you reach.** My healthcare posts underreach everything else, 19% versus 29%, and they're staying in the rotation because the smaller audience they find is the one that sends the leads. Judge every post by the log from step one, not by the dashboard LinkedIn shows you.

The tactics will drift as the algorithm does. The KPI won't. The right people knowing how you think, before you need them to, is the only job security left. Build that.

# Meta still has widest social media reach

Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp each have more than 3 billion users, giving the platforms’ owner a clear lead in the digital community landscape.

 Published July 26, 2026 

By

[Andrew Hutchinson](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/editors/adhutchinson/)Content and Social Media Manager

Meta remains the leader of the pack in terms of total social platform reach and usage, while Threads continues to gain on X and Pinterest continues to rise. The information comes from the latest snapshot of overall users, as measured by app.

This is worth noting not only in terms of reach, but also in regards to where attention is shifting. The data can help brands and marketers think about where to spend promotional budgets, and also serves as a measure of general online trends.

![Image 21: Social media app users - July 2026](https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/4LPiCxYSstroa4IMU3qjmm1o94D7L17coiFm-ubgJjo/g:ce/rs:fit:1600:0/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS9zb2NpYWxfbWVkaWFfTUFVX2NvdW50c19KdW5lXzIwMjYucG5n.webp)

As shown in this chart, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp have all reached 3 billion monthly active users, based on the platform’s own reporting.

While Meta no longer shares platform-specific numbers in its quarterly performance update anymore, it does share milestone achievements. Per the company, Instagram is the most recent of Meta’s owned apps to reach the 3 billion user milestone, which it hit in [September 2025](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/instagram-reaches-3-billion-users-ui-update/761038/). Meta shared that WhatsApp reached 3 billion users in its [Q1 2025 earnings call](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/meta-adds-more-users-revenue-q1-2025/746823/), while Facebook hit that mark [in 2023](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/meta-posts-strong-q2-result-facebook-crosses-3-billion-monthly-active-users/689108/).

However, Meta only reports its total family of apps usage number, which is a combined total of unique users across all of its platforms. In Q1 2026, Meta reported [3.56 billion total users](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/metas-daily-active-user-count-declined-in-q1-2026/818904/), which was a slight decline on its previous quarterly report, and the first decline in its overall user count since the company began reporting numbers.

That could suggest that Meta’s apps have lost some of their allure. Even so, more than 3 billion people — nearly a third of the world’s population — are still logging into one or more Meta apps every month.

Meta’s Messenger app sees 1.3 billion monthly actives, according to [official reporting](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/social-networks/facebook-reveals-messenger-day-usage-data-messenger-climbs-13b-mau) from the company, and Threads reached 500 million actives [just last month](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/threads-reaches-500m-user-milestone/823099/).

YouTube is just behind Meta, based on reporting from [Business of Apps](https://www.businessofapps.com/data/youtube-statistics/?_sp=0bf67436-18e0-4fcb-bbf4-4585efb25b8f), which reported that the platform has 2.7 billion monthly active users.

YouTube is generally pretty guarded about its official user counts, though it reported significant increases in Shorts views, which rose from [about 30 billion daily views in 2022](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/youtube-shorts-now-up-to-30-billion-daily-views-ads-in-shorts-now-in-testi/622814/) to[about 200 billion daily views](https://www.businessofapps.com/data/youtube-statistics/?_sp=0bf67436-18e0-4fcb-bbf4-4585efb25b8f) in 2026.

TikTok said it reached [one billion monthly actives in 2021](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/tiktok-reaches-a-billion-active-users-the-latest-milestone-for-the-app/607248/), although Business of Apps reported that the platform reached [1.6 billion MAU in 2023](https://www.businessofapps.com/data/tik-tok-statistics/?_sp=0bf67436-18e0-4fcb-bbf4-4585efb25b8f). It’s worth noting, however, that TikTok itself hasn’t shared any official usage data to confirm either number.

TikTok has also been hit with restrictions in some regions, and those may have potentially limited its growth.

Meanwhile, Snapchat is closing in on its first billion, with the platform reaching[956 million in Q1 2026](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/snapchat-usage-declined-in-the-us-and-eu-in-q1/819535/). The platform has seen significant growth in India, where it’s become a key connector for young users.

The ranking of Pinterest here may be a surprise to some, with the platform now up to[631 million monthly actives](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/pinterest-posts-solid-growth-for-the-first-quarter-of-2026/819391/).

X is almost neck-and-neck with Threads, with [550 million MAU](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/spacex-filing-provides-insight-into-x-grok-and-xai/820945/).

Reddit doesn’t report monthly active user counts, but the company [reported 126.8 million daily active users](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/reddit-posts-strong-q1-results/819150/) for the first quarter of 2026, up from 121.4 million in Q4 2025. An estimated 500,000 weekly actives is extrapolated from that, although Reddit’s actual monthly active figure may be higher.

LinkedIn also doesn’t share active user numbers. Instead, it reports its full member count, which is currently at [1.3 billion](https://news.linkedin.com/about-us?_sp=0bf67436-18e0-4fcb-bbf4-4585efb25b8f). But LinkedIn’s[EU reporting data](https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1678508?_sp=0bf67436-18e0-4fcb-bbf4-4585efb25b8f) indicates that around 32% of EU LinkedIn members are actively using the app each month. That suggests that LinkedIn currently serves around 416 million monthly active users.

Of course, total user counts are not especially meaningful in a broader context, because what really matters is where the most relevant audience is for brand campaigns and messaging. With so many niche discussions and groups, that could mean every platform will have some value for outreach and engagement.

But in terms of broader trends, it is interesting to note where the platforms are placed, and which ones are leading the way in overall growth and presence.

It’s also worth noting that while only some platforms share their daily active user counts, the average conversion rate is around 2.05 times fewer than monthly counts, based on official reports.

That means that if brands want to estimate daily active user counts for any social app, they will need to divide the monthly number by 2.05 to get an estimate of their likely audience. The only significant outlier is Reddit, which sees 3.8 times more weekly users than daily users.

# Hilton’s CMO on why brand marketing is an ‘irrational affinity business’

Global CMO Mark Weinstein explains how the hospitality titan is utilizing creators, AI and loyalty in an evolving advertising landscape.

 Published July 28, 2026

Despite rising costs on everything from gas to groceries, U.S. consumers are still prioritizing travel this summer. While some consumers are traveling closer to home or choosing less expensive destinations to save money, about one-fifth are using loyalty points or rewards to keep costs low, [according to a recent survey](https://www.hoteldive.com/news/travelers-creative-ways-summer-trips-ahla-report/825637/?_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f) from the American Hotel & Lodging Association.

Hilton is doing its part to make loyalty easier: The hospitality titan last month launched a social-first campaign to dole out 1 billion Hilton Honors points. The effort kicked off in Instagram posts featuring [Paris Hilton](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZckE9DOIwz/?hl=en&_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f) and Formula One star [Lando Norris](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZsXd3KMJbz/?hl=en&_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f). The sweepstakes, which runs through July 30, is an opportunity for Hilton to tap into pop culture and consumer passions in an organic way. After all, who better to “give away” the points than the brand’s most famous ambassador and a driver whose McLaren Formula 1 Team has been partnered with Hilton for more than 20 years?

“It’s taking their expertise and imparting it upon their fans,” Hilton Global CMO Mark Weinstein said of the effort. “It’s a fun way to tap into the summer narrative that’s out there, but also be back in culture and conversation, in a way that’s authentic to who we are, versus just doing a bunch of giveaways.”

The effort spotlights a Hilton Honors program that has 260 million members and demonstrates how the marketer is approaching loyalty. While extra nights, free upgrades and experiential opportunities like the ones offered [through new cruise partner Explora Journeys](https://stories.hilton.com/releases/hilton-and-explora-journeys-announce-luxury-ocean-travel-partnership-debut-of-hilton-honors-adventures?_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f) are key rewards in the program, loyalty is more emotional than transactional, Weinstein maintains.

“You wouldn’t want the tenth bagel for free if the first nine weren’t very good,” he said. “You don’t win loyalty from earning points. You earn it from redeeming points. You don’t earn it from earning tiers. You earn it from the value of the tiers being delivered.”

Hilton in Q2 2026 saw system-wide comparable revenue per available room, a key industry metric, increase 3.9% compared to the same period in 2025, [per an earnings report released Tuesday](https://stories-editor.hilton.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Q2-2026-Earnings-Release.pdf?_gl=1*1g6rr8b*_gcl_au*MTQyNDE4OTA1NS4xNzg0NjYyOTIwLi0uLS4xNzg0NjYzMzc1LjY2Mzg1MTAzMC4xNzg1MTYzMDY0LjE3ODUxNjMwNjM.&_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f). The company raised its outlook for annual revenue per available room growth to between 3% and 3.5%, with benefits from the World Cup in the third quarter being offset by the midterm elections in the fourth quarter.

“We’re not in the commodity business,” the executive added. “We’re in the irrational affinity business.”

### Creators on a brand platform

Aside from famous brand ambassadors, Hilton has also leaned into the creator economy, which is on track to generate $44 billion in U.S. ad spending this year and is now a “[core media channel](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/creator-marketing-now-a-core-media-channel-while-search-slows-iab/817832/),” according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Using creators requires brands like Hilton to give up control over its narrative in exchange for immediacy, Weinstein said.

“It doesn’t always come out exactly how you would perfectly script it, but you’re betting on the authenticity and the resonance that [creator content] has with their audience is enough of a benefit … that you’re going to take that risk with your brand,” he said. “It can be a little nerve-wracking as a CMO and a brand leader.”

Hilton’s work with creators has developed alongside the evolution of the space. Early creator partners, including some micro-creators, were trying to make their own versions of TV commercials, perhaps due to brand briefs that were too prescriptive.

“If you want to be in those forums, you’ve got to trust creators to know their audience well enough to know how they’ll best receive the message, and that means a little bit of tarnish sometimes,” Weinstein said.

The focus on trust is used whether dealing with a creator with 10,000 followers or 10 million followers, and it arrives as creator marketing continues to see a greater share of production and media budgets that were formerly reserved for traditional advertising. Weinstein attributes some of Hilton’s ability to cede creative control to the [strength of its global brand platform](https://www.hoteldive.com/news/mark-weinstein-hilton-for-the-stay/700974/?_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f), “For the Stay,” that launched in 2022.

“That’s why having a brand platform matters so much: because you’re no longer trying to hit it out of the park every single time,” Weinstein said. “Content has never been cheaper to produce. The need to get people’s attention has never been higher. If you can de-risk that environment, you actually hit some singles and doubles that turn into home runs.”

### The role of AI evolves

As global CMO, Weinstein oversees brand and performance marketing for a portfolio of 28 brands totaling more than 9,200 hotels across 144 countries and territories. As expected, artificial intelligence is playing a role in helping Hilton meet its marketing imperatives. The tech is “rapidly transforming” Hilton’s ability to keep its inventory of rooms up-to-date, with accurate images and descriptions, so that it is bookable and advertisable, the executive said.

“We have a large team of people that supports that. They were always behind the eight ball when it comes to trying to have 1.3 million rooms up to date all the time. Having technology to scale that is quite impactful for us. Not just to automate it, but actually to use the AI capabilities to help us through that,” he explained.

AI is also bringing down the cost of performance marketing and giving Hilton the ability to generate thousands of variations on campaigns that can be more personalized and customized than ever — a necessity in a category where a brand can go from irrelevant to relevant in as little as 10 seconds, depending on consumer needs.

“When somebody books their hotel, that customer’s gone, so our ability to use AI to respond in that moment to piece together the right asset, to ship it, to buy the media — that is a competitive game changer for sure,” Weinstein said.

Beyond content creation, the next frontier of AI is discoverability across tools that, in some cases, are replacing search as the gateway to travel planning. Already, more than one-third of Americans planning to travel this summer are [using AI to help them plan their vacations](https://www.hoteldive.com/news/artificial-intelligence-mainstream-travel-planning-tool/826002/?_sp=a5bc731f-097c-43f8-984d-ec2823d33a2f), per Allianz’s Global Travel Confidence Index with polling from Ipsos.
